title: Calibrated uncertainty quantification for prosumer flexibility aggregation in ancillary service markets
source: ScienceDirect Publication: Applied Energy
abstract: Reliable forecasting of prosumer flexibility is critical for demand response aggregators participating in frequency controlled ancillary services market, where strict reliability requirements such as the P90 standard are enforced. Limited historical data, dependence on exogeneous factors, and heterogenous prosumer behaviour introduce significant epistemic uncertainty, making deterministic or poorly calibrated probabilistic models unsuitable for market bidding. This paper proposes the use of scalable uncertainty quantification framework that integrates Monte Carlo dropout (MCD) with conformal prediction (CP) to produce calibrated, finite sample prediction intervals for aggregated prosumer flexibility. The proposed framework is applied to a behind-the-meter aggregator participating in the Danish manual frequency restoration reserve capacity market. A large-scale synthetic dataset is generated using a modified industry-grade home energy management system, combined with publicly available load, solar, price, activation and device-level data. The resulting machine learning surrogate model captures aggregate prosumer price responsiveness and provides uncertainty-aware estimates suitable for market bidding. Multiple multivariate CP strategies are evaluated and benchmarked against conventional MCD-based methods. Results show that standalone MCD systematically overestimates available flexibility and violates P90 compliance, whereas the proposed MCD-CP framework achieves reliable coverage with controlled conservatism. When embedded in aggregator bidding model, conformalised methods substantially reduce overbidding risk and achieve upto 70% of perfect-information profit while satisfying regulatory reliability constraints, providing practical, computationally efficient, and market-compliant solution for aggregator flexibility forecasting under uncertainty.

title: Label-efficient global centralized and distributed photovoltaic segmentation via hierarchical CLIP-calibrated active learning
source: ScienceDirect Publication: Applied Energy
abstract: Accurate global photovoltaic (PV) mapping is essential for renewable energy planning, grid integration, and carbon-neutral transition assessment. AI-based remote sensing segmentation offers an efficient way to update PV inventories, but pixel-wise annotation of PV imagery remains expensive at large scale, especially across distributed rooftop systems and centralized utility-scale plants with different resolutions and geographic backgrounds. A key practical challenge is therefore to achieve high-accuracy PV segmentation with the smallest possible annotation budget under realistic labeling constraints. To address this challenge, we propose a hierarchical CLIP-calibrated active learning (AL) strategy for label-efficient global PV segmentation. Due to the heterogeneous appearance of PV scenes, CLIP is introduced as an external visual-semantic calibrator, and sample acquisition is organized into three stages: semantic coverage in the CLIP feature space, hybrid-uncertainty hard-example mining, and feature-level redundancy removal. Using SegFormer-B3 as the segmentation baseline, we evaluate the method on two worldwide benchmarks covering distributed rooftop PV at 0.1–1.0 m resolution and centralized utility-scale PV at 10–20 m resolution. Under the same annotation budget, our method consistently outperforms classic AL baselines, including Entropy, BALD, and Core-set, across both benchmarks. Practical deployment analysis shows that, for an IoU ≥ 90 % target, our method reduces the required annotation budget by 39.1–78.8% for distributed PV and 15.1–34.8% for centralized PV, corresponding to estimated manual-labeling savings of approximately 260 h/$5.2k and 114 h/$2.28k relative to Random sampling, respectively. These results support scalable, low-cost PV inventory updates for deployment monitoring, grid planning, and renewable energy planning under constrained labeling resources.

title: Spatiotemporal analysis of global future photovoltaic potential and its driving mechanisms
source: ScienceDirect Publication: Applied Energy
abstract: Accurate estimation of photovoltaic (PV) potential under future climate scenarios is critical for global decarbonization and energy transition planning. This study employed the Global Solar Energy Estimation model to calculate PV potential and carbon mitigation across three Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs) using calibrated data of 2015–2100 from the CMIP6 data based on the Bayesian Model Averaging method. Results showed that the global annual mean PV capacity factor (CF) (power generation) was 0.1622 (2010 TWh), 0.1597 (1993 TWh), and 0.1543 (1961 TWh) under low (SSP1-2.6), intermediate (SSP2-4.5), and high (SSP5-8.5) carbon emission scenarios, respectively. Correspondingly, 33%, 12%, and 8% of global land area exhibited significant increases in CFs. Experiments of climate impacts on PV potential revealed that a reduction in PV CF (power generation) of 0.0008 (1 TWh) per decade under high carbon emission scenario, driven by a decline in surface solar radiation from increased aerosols and cloud cover, along with panel efficiency losses from rising air temperature. Investigation of physical factors on PV potential indicated that the advanced crystalline silicon materials and two-axis panel tracking systems demonstrated substantial potential in enhancing PV power generation and carbon mitigation. Moreover, the driving mechanisms of the climate variables on PV potential was also investigated based on the Structural Equation Modeling method. Our findings quantify the potential of PV technology in generation and decarbonization, assisting in policy development in energy transitions to address climate change.

title: Structural basis of TACO1 function in mitochondrial translation elongation
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Protein synthesis depends on specialized regulatory factors to overcome difficult-to-translate sequences during elongation that cause ribosomal stalling. In human mitochondria, this function is carried out by TACO1 (Translation activator of COX1). Here, we report the cryo-electron microscopy structure of human TACO1 bound to the mitoribosome, revealing its mechanistic role as a dedicated elongation regulator. Unlike the prokaryotic elongation factor EF-P and the eukaryotic eIF5A, which bind the ribosomal E site and stabilize P-site tRNA to facilitate peptide bond formation, TACO1 adopts a distinct strategy. It binds near the A site, closely interacting with the Sarcin Ricin loop and the L7/L12 stalk, similar to general translation elongation factors, such as EF-Tumt and mtEF-G1mt, and contacts the A-site tRNA. Using AlphaFold analysis and molecular dynamics simulations, we further show how a series of conformational changes allow its N-terminal domain to reorient and transiently engage with the A-site tRNA via a conserved and functionally critical basic amino acid patch. The bacterial homolog of TACO1, namely YebC2, shares the structural features required for its function. Overall, we present an evolutionarily conserved mechanism employed by TACO1 to enhance mitochondrial translation efficiency.

title: Interface engineering of Pt-based catalysts toward enhanced methanol oxidation in direct methanol fuel cells
source: ScienceDirect Publication: Applied Energy
abstract: Direct methanol fuel cells (DMFCs) are promising power sources, but their practical performance remains limited by sluggish methanol oxidation, CO poisoning, Pt-site degradation, and low Pt utilization. This review critically examines Pt-centered interface engineering for the methanol oxidation reaction (MOR) in DMFC anodes. First, MOR pathways, performance descriptors, in situ and operando methods, and the factors governing the transfer of half-cell activity to DMFC output are assessed. Representative catalysts are then compared according to the dominant kinetic or degradation limitation addressed by their local interfaces, covering adsorption regulation, pathway control, oxygen-species cooperation, Pt-site retention or regeneration, and cooperative low-Pt utilization. The analysis assigns the dominant function of multifunctional interfaces, evaluates that function using process-specific evidence, and determines whether it survives working-state evolution and membrane electrode assembly integration. Cross-case comparison shows that material class does not uniquely define function and that similar activity, CO tolerance, or durability may arise from different mechanisms. It further distinguishes suppression of adsorbed CO (CO ads) formation from oxidation of pre-adsorbed CO ads , nominal oxophilicity from verified water activation, and structural retention from functional retention and controlled regeneration. Finally, problem-matched design rules are proposed for efficient, low-Pt, and durable DMFC anodes.

title: Temporal strain-resolved metagenomics associates IBD dysbiosis with gastrointestinal inflammation
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: The gut microbiome in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is enriched in proinflammatory bacteria, yet defining a consistent dysbiotic signature is challenging, due to substantial variation between individuals and over time. We performed a high-resolution meta-analysis of 4,839 public metagenomes to disentangle the effects of IBD subtypes, inflammation, temporal, and individual variability. After accounting for temporal variation, we show that IBD-associated dysbiosis was characterized primarily by relative depletion of commensal bacteria rather than expansion of disease-associated taxa, together with increased microbiome variability both within and between individuals. Although 30% of species were IBD-associated, only 73% of these associations remained consistent across all timepoints. IBD-associated bacteria showed reduced persistence within hosts, increased strain loss and diminished strain engraftment. 8% of commensal species displayed strain-level associations with IBD that were independent of species-level changes, suggesting distinct ecological strategies for persistence. Finally, defining an inflammatory index, we demonstrated that inflammation explains much of the observed variation in microbial composition and abundance. Together, our findings indicate that inflammation associates and likely contributes to loss of commensals, thereby limiting microbiome recovery and resilience.

title: Chronic TFE3 activation in TFE3-associated neurodevelopmental disorder drives metabolic rigidity, lysosomal failure, and cell-extracellular matrix destabilization
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: The transcription factor TFE3 coordinates cellular adaptation to stress. While its acute activation is cytoprotective, chronic TFE3 dysregulation is linked to diverse pathologies. Here, we characterize the cellular landscape of TFE3-NDD, a recently described neurodevelopmental disorder caused by mutations that disrupt the TFE3-Rag GTPase interface, leading to constitutive TFE3 nuclear localization. Using patient-derived fibroblasts, we show that TFE3-NDD is primarily a metabolic and homeostatic disorder. Mutant cells undergo a profound rewiring toward oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), resulting in metabolic rigidity and a vulnerability to energy failure. Despite a massive expansion of the lysosomal compartment, we observe a paradoxical qualitative failure characterized by impaired acidification, defective protease maturation, increased lysosomal exocytosis, and aberrant cathepsin K secretion. This secretory phenotype is coupled with a destabilized cell-extracellular matrix interface, marked by impaired migration, defective coordination between actomyosin tension and focal adhesion maturation, and a loss of synaptic stabilizers. Notably, TFE3-NDD shares a signature of high OXPHOS and ferroptosis resistance with TFE3-dependent cancers, such as translocation renal cell carcinoma. Our findings reveal how the chronic hyperactivation of a protective stress-response factor collapses cellular homeostasis, providing a mechanistic framework for the tissue malformations and neurodevelopmental deficits that define TFE3-NDD.

title: High-content morphological profiling by Cell Painting in 3D spheroids
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Cell Painting is a popular high-content imaging assay that captures the shape and internal organization of 2D cell cultures at scale. While 3D cell cultures are more physiologically relevant models – especially for studying drug perturbations – they remain challenging to image because light scatters before it reaches the cultures’ interior. Here, we introduce a scalable method to adapt Cell Painting for 3D spheroids. We show that tissue-clearing, a technique that makes spheroids transparent, combined with a focusing routine that locates spheroids on the fly, enables Cell Painting at single-cell level inside intact spheroids. By profiling 52 clinically relevant drugs, we show that single-cell fingerprints clustered by biological pathway and resolved drug effects more robustly than those of flattened spheroid-wide views. Notably, the effect of two drugs, 5-fluorouracil and olaparib, nearly indistinguishable in 2D monolayers, diverged in spheroids. This finding was then corroborated by DNA-damage, cell-cycle, and gene-expression assays. The workflow runs on a spinning-disk confocal microscope in a standard 384-well plate format, making single-cell 3D profiling accessible to laboratories already performing Cell Painting.

title: 2D-PELSA maps multidimensional target landscapes and reveals E2-GPX4 engagement associated with ferroptosis
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Current methods for mapping ligand-protein interactions struggle to resolve weak yet critical binding events and conformational dynamics, particularly for pleiotropic endogenous hormones. Here, we develop a peptide-centric, dose-resolved strategy, the two-dimensional peptide-centric local stability assay (2D-PELSA), which enables highly reliable target identification and direct estimation of local binding affinities in native cellular environments. Dose-dependent information converts static proteolysis signatures into quantitative readouts of local structural remodeling at enhanced resolution, resolving direct engagement, allosteric regulation, complex remodeling, etc. Applied to 17β-estradiol (E2)-treated BT474 breast cancer cell lysates, 2D-PELSA identifies 1288 conformotypic E2-responsive peptides and 24 candidate targets enriched in unsaturated and long-chain fatty acid metabolism with micromolar EC50 values. GPX4 is identified as an E2-engaged ferroptosis regulator with an EC50 of 2.4 μM and is downregulated by micromolar E2. Orthogonal Western blot and MS-based assays validate this interaction in lysates and living cells. Integrated proteomic, lipidomic and phenotypic analyses show that chronic micromolar E2 exposure induces lipid metabolic reprogramming, lipid peroxidation and oxidative, iron-dependent cell death that is only partially rescued by ferrostatin-1 or deferoxamine. These findings establish 2D-PELSA as a versatile platform for dissecting ligand-induced structural responses and mapping target landscapes in complex biological contexts.

title: Inter‑symbiont horizontal gene transfer and functional partitioning in globally sampled lichen metagenomes
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Horizontal gene transfer (HGT) is a fundamental eco‑evolutionary process, yet its functional and symbiotic significance in lichens remains poorly understood. Here, using 197 high‑completeness eukaryotic metagenome-assembled genomes derived from 533 lichen-associated metagenomes sampled across six continents, we detect 1,882 putative HGT‑acquired genes among ~1.6 million predicted genes (~0.12%) across the major symbiotic partners, most of which were of bacterial origin. This dataset enables us to test two hypotheses: (H1) HGT-acquired genes exhibit partner-specific functional profiles consistent with functional differentiation between the major symbiotic partners, and (H2) inter‑symbiont HGT has occurred across the fungal–algal interface. Consistent with H1, putative HGT‑acquired genes in mycobionts show greater representation of functions related to cell wall/membrane/envelope biogenesis, transcription, and defense mechanisms, whereas putative HGT‑acquired genes in photobionts show greater representation of functions related to amino acid transport and metabolism, signal transduction, and translation. Consistent with H2, we detect 31 putative inter‑symbiont HGT-acquired genes (16 inferred from mycobionts to photobionts and 15 inferred from photobionts to mycobionts), including multiple photobiont genes inferred to encode RfeF transcription factors with putative mycobiont origin, suggesting a potential contribution of HGT to regulatory evolution. These findings are consistent with a potential role of HGT in functional specialization and potential gene flow across fungal–algal boundaries, offering insights into the eco‑evolutionary dynamics of symbiotic systems.

title: PARG inhibition elicits cytotoxicity by sequestering XRCC1 and other PAR-binding proteins into PAR-dependent nuclear condensates
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: DNA breaks activate PARP1/2 to synthesize poly(ADP-ribose) (PAR), which relax chromatin and recruit DNA repair factors. PAR is normally short-lived and rapidly degraded by poly(ADP-ribose) glycohydrolase (PARG). While PARP1/2 inhibitors target homologous recombination (HR)-deficient cancers, predictive biomarkers for PARG inhibition (PARGi) remain undefined. Using genome-wide CRISPR screens, we find that PARGi is synthetically lethal with loss of multiple PAR-binding factors (XRCC1-LIG3/POLB, ALC1/CHD1L, ARH3, PARG itself) but not HR-deficiency. Conversely, loss of PARP1, NMNAT1 (nuclear NAD⁺ synthesis), or UNG confers resistance. Mechanistically, PARGi induces reversible PARP1- and PAR-dependent nuclear condensates in undamaged cells. While lacking detectable DNA breaks, these condensates sequester various PAR-binding proteins (e.g. XRCC1, ALC1, FUS), reducing their nuclear availability and impairing recruitment to bona fide DNA lesions. These findings identify PAR-binding protein sequestration as the mechanism underlying PARGi cytotoxicity, explain the paradoxical essentiality of PARG but not PARP1, and establish PAR-binding factor deficiency as a biomarker for PARGi.

title: Lipids intercalate and mediate multi-channel assemblies of connexin-46/50 gap junctions
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Gap junction channels enable direct electrical and metabolic exchange between adjacent cells and organize into plaques containing tens to thousands of channels. Although plaque formation modulates junctional conductance, the structural basis for channel–channel organization remains poorly defined. Here, we reconstitute native lens connexin-46/50 (Cx46/50) channels into MSP-based lipid nanodiscs containing multiple channels and determine high-resolution structures of dual-channel assemblies in two configurations. The interfaces lack extensive protein–protein contacts and instead contain ordered lipid densities that define much of the inter-channel interface. These interfaces stabilize discrete lipid populations, including an interstitial lipid near the N-terminal gating domain, suggesting how channel organization may promote lipid occupancy near the pore. We also refine the Cx46/50 single-channel structure to 1.8 Å, providing an internal reference and chemical detail of the stabilized open-state. Together, these results define lipid-rich interfaces as a feature of multi-channel organization and suggest how plaque-like packing may tune gap junction function.

title: Silk fibroin intrinsically activates Ccl27⁺ migratory-paracrine keratinocytes to orchestrate epidermal–dermal crosstalk for regenerative wound healing
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Rapid and functional skin wound healing remains a major clinical challenge, while current biomaterial-based therapies largely serve as passive scaffolds or delivery vehicles. Whether biomaterials possess intrinsic bioactivities that instruct endogenous regenerative programs remains unclear. Here, independent of bulk structural/mechanical cues or exogenous biomolecules, we show that silk fibroin (SF), a clinically approved biomaterial, intrinsically programs keratinocytes into a Ccl27⁺ migratory-paracrine pro-regenerative state that coordinates epidermal-dermal crosstalk to drive regenerative wound healing. Integrated scRNA-seq, proteomics, and genetic perturbation reveal that SF engages keratinocyte ITGA2 to activate PI3K-Akt signaling and relieve P53-mediated Ccl27 repression. Elevated Ccl27 enhances keratinocyte migration and re-epithelialization, while its secretion from SF-activated keratinocytes promotes fibroblast proliferation and dermal remodeling, collectively enabling wound closure and appendage reconstruction. Keratinocyte-specific Ccl27 knockdown largely abrogates SF-mediated regeneration in vivo. These findings uncover the intrinsic bioactivity of SF and establish biomaterials as instructive cues rather than passive scaffolds for functional tissue repair.

title: Preferred evolutionary routes of convergence in Klebsiella pneumoniae favor siderophore acquisition over hypervirulence
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: The rise of Klebsiella pneumoniae combining antimicrobial resistance and virulence genes poses a major health threat, but the evolutionary routes and phenotypic consequences of this convergence are poorly understood. Here, phylogenetics of 1468 isolates and population analysis of 7520 plasmids, from >50 countries through the last two decades, reveal that convergence follows preferred, constrained evolutionary paths. The dominant route involves multidrug-resistant classical K. pneumoniae acquiring conjugative IncFIB(Mar)/IncHI1B(Mar) plasmids carrying an incomplete set of virulence biomarkers. Across 25 independent convergence events, the acquisition of the aerobactin siderophore locus was the only universal feature. These convergent isolates exhibit enhanced siderophore production but consistently lack the hypervirulent phenotype in vivo. In contrast, genuine hypervirulent strains that gain resistance remain rare. We conclude that enhanced siderophore production, not hypervirulence, is the primary adaptive trait driving the success of globally emerging convergent lineages, representing a distinct evolutionary state optimized for transmission rather than systemic invasion.

title: Concentration‑dependent switching between ligand‑like and solvent‑like lipid regulation in a model ion channel
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Cell membranes are not only protective barriers but also active chemical environments that regulate protein structure and function. However, how individual lipid species influence membrane proteins across physiological concentration ranges, either as specific ligands or through bilayer-mediated solvent effects, remains poorly defined. Here, using the cyclic nucleotide-gated ion channel SthK reconstituted into defined membranes, we show that phosphatidic acid enhances channel activity across all tested concentrations but, at low mole fractions ( ~ 0.7-1 mol%), it selectively and cooperatively increases agonist potency, meeting criteria for a site‑specific allosteric ligand. In contrast, the zwitterionic lipid phosphatidylethanolamine modulates SthK activity exclusively through linear, solvent‑like effects across the same concentration range. Structural analysis reveals that low anionic lipid content expands the closed‑state conformational ensemble without promoting pore opening, providing a structural basis for lipid-dependent latent allostery. Together, these results establish lipid concentration as a governing regulatory variable that quantitatively distinguishes ligand‑like from solvent‑like mechanisms of membrane protein regulation.

title: DNA CODEC: compressed obfuscated DNA encoding in cells for secure in vivo data storage
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: DNA represents a compelling medium for data storage due to its density, durability, and compatibility with biological systems. Current in vivo DNA data storage strategies are largely restricted to single-population systems, limiting scalability and access control. Here, we present DNA CODEC, a multi-population in vivo DNA data storage platform that combines high-density encoding with molecular obfuscation across engineered human cell populations. CODEC uses 10-ary Huffman coding with degenerate bases to optimize compressibility while maintaining decoding accuracy despite biological and technical noise. Data payloads are stably integrated into the human genome using CRISPR-based targeted insertion. Obfuscation is introduced through heterogeneous populations containing decoy clones with structurally similar, non-informative masking sequences to conceal the true payload. CODEC stably maintains genomic payloads across extended cell culture, demonstrating robustness to replication errors and population drift. Together, these features establish a scalable framework for high-fidelity and secure DNA data storage in biological systems.

title: Tumor-intrinsic PTPN12 suppresses anti-tumor immunity in colorectal cancer by restraining a dual epigenetic and cytoskeletal dsRNA sensing program
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Innate sensing of endogenous double-stranded RNA and the ensuing interferon response are crucial for the efficacy of immune checkpoint inhibition. Microsatellite stable colorectal cancer characteristically lacks this response, remaining immune-refractory with undefined intrinsic regulators. Here, through an in vivo clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats screen, we identify PTPN12 as a physiological barrier that suppresses double-stranded RNA sensing and interferon response. TRIM28 was identified as a direct PTPN12 substrate here; PTPN12 removes phosphorylation at Y370 to stabilize repressive complexes and silence transposable elements, while concurrently rewiring the adhesive cytoskeleton to disrupt the spatially organization of cytosolic double-stranded RNA required for efficient innate sensing. Pharmacological inducible PTPN12 knockdown inhibits pre-established tumor growth and overcomes immunotherapy resistance in vivo, recapitulating PTPN12 ablation-induced massive double-stranded RNA accumulation. Our findings reveal a role for PTPN12 in coupling epigenetic silencing with cytoskeletal surveillance, suggesting potential strategies to augment anti-tumor immunity and overcome immunotherapy resistance in microsatellite stable colorectal cancer.

title: Harnessing a Light-Activated Ruthenium(II) Complex Self-Delivery Nanoplatform for Tumor–Organelle Cascade-Targeted Immunotherapy via Type II Immunogenic Cell Death
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Immunogenic cell death (ICD) converts immunosuppressive “cold” tumors into immunogenic “hot” ones, yet ICD inducers with precise tumor–organelle cascade targeting and spatiotemporal controllability remain largely unexplored. Herein, we report a self-delivery nanoplatform (ER-Ru NPs) constructed via the self-assembly of well-defined tumor–endoplasmic reticulum (ER) cascade-targeting ruthenium(II) complexes. The intrinsic amphiphilicity enables self-assembly of the ruthenium(II) complexes into stabilized nanoparticles with efficient tumor accumulation properties via biotin-mediated active targeting, without any exogenous carriers. Following cellular internalization, the released ruthenium(II) complex monomer specifically accumulates in the ER to generate a cleaved Ru–H2O anticancer agent and in situ reactive oxygen species (ROS) upon red-light irradiation. The robust ROS burst triggers severe ER stress via activation of the PERK/eIF2α pathway, leading to the release of damage-associated molecular patterns and the type II ICD induction. Notably, this cascade-targeted ICD activation strategy enhances not only tumor specificity but also the immunogenicity of dying tumor cells, achieving effective primary tumor ablation in the 4T1 models and simultaneously suppressing distant tumors through dendritic cell maturation, cytotoxic T-cell infiltration, and memory T-cell generation. This study offers a paradigm for photoactivatable, self-delivery ICD inducers with cascade targeting, holding substantial promise for clinical translation in precision cancer immunotherapy.

title: IRAK4 autophosphorylation functions as a molecular switch to regulate death domain assembly and Myddosome maturation
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: The organization of signaling proteins into multi-component complexes is essential for innate immune responses and is often achieved through the oligomerization of death domains (DDs). The Myddosome, composed of MyD88 and IRAK family kinases, exemplifies this mechanism. However, how DDs assemble in an ordered and regulated manner to form Myddosomes to control signaling output remains unclear. Here, we show that IRAK4 kinase activity and autophosphorylation are required for IRAK4:IRAK1 heterotypic DD interactions. We show that IRAK1 is autoinhibited by its kinase domain, and IRAK4 phosphorylation relieves this inhibition, enabling IRAK1 DD incorporation into Myddosomes. This phosphorylation-dependent switch similarly controls IRAK2/3 incorporation. Thus, IRAK4 autophosphorylation acts as an energy-dependent molecular switch that integrates phosphorylation with protein oligomerization to drive Myddosome maturation and signal transduction. This mechanism demonstrates how enzymatic activity can impose temporal and spatial control over macromolecular assembly to ensure directional and context-dependent inflammatory signaling.

title: Interface Engineering of Hydrated Tungsten Oxide via Carbon Nitride for Durable Electrochromic Energy Storage
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Electrochromic smart windows demand high optical contrast, fast switching, long-term durability, and charge-storage functionality, yet hydrated tungsten oxides suffer from restricted ion transport and structural degradation during repeated ion insertion/extraction. Here, we present a carbon nitride-driven phase transformation strategy for a durable energy-storing electrochromic hydrated tungsten oxide. Under mild hydrogen annealing, orthorhombic WO3·H2O nanoplates containing an optimized 10 wt % carbon nitride (CNx) selectively transform into predominantly hexagonal WO3·0.33H2O nanorods (∼80%), accompanied by a relatively minor orthorhombic fraction (∼20%). The CNx promotes structural rearrangement while providing nitrogen-rich Li+-interactive sites that regulate interfacial ion transport and improve electrochemical reversibility. Supported by density functional theory, impedance, diffusion, and postcycling analyses, the optimized WHX-CNx10% film shows favorable Li+ insertion, improved charge-transfer kinetics, and excellent structural retention. The air spray-coated film in 3-electrode system delivers 57% optical modulation at 650 nm, coloration/bleaching times of 2.9/0.6 s, stable cycling over 20,000 cycles, and an areal capacitance of 16.9 mF/cm2. A 5 × 5 cm2 device further exhibits optical modulation of 52% at 650 nm with a coloration efficiency of ∼156 cm2/C. These results establish CNx-mediated phase and interface engineering as an effective route toward scalable, durable, and energy-storing electrochromic smart windows.

title: Multimodal precision diagnostics in clinical xenotransplantation
source: Nature
abstract: Recent breakthroughs in pig-to-human xenotransplantation have successfully prevented hyperacute rejection of kidney, heart, liver and lung xenografts, marking a milestone long considered a critical barrier. However, these major advances also brought new challenges into focus, as immune-mediated graft injuries including antibody-mediated rejection, T cell-mediated rejection and innate immune activation have been observed in most xenotransplantation procedures to date. Detection and management of these injuries remain a critical bottleneck, as conventional histopathology and standard clinical monitoring lack the sensitivity required to identify subclinical injury early enough to guide timely intervention. This diagnostic gap underscores an urgent need for the development of advanced, multimodal precision diagnostic frameworks to enhance immune surveillance, which will be essential for standardizing clinical protocols and enabling pathogenesis-driven therapeutic intervention. This approach will inform both immunosuppressive regimens and future gene editing strategies aimed at engineering rejection-resistant porcine organs, ultimately prolonging graft survival. Broad adoption of such an integrative strategy will be essential to transition xenotransplantation from an experimental intervention into a safe, scalable and patient-centred clinical therapy. In this Review, we synthesize recent progress in xenotransplantation and position multimodal precision diagnostics as a pivotal strategy to address the remaining immunological and clinical barriers to widespread clinical implementation.

title: The contribution of salt marshes to wave attenuation during extreme storms
source: Nature
abstract: Salt marshes protect coastlines by attenuating wind waves with their elevated marsh platform and above-ground vegetation1. Confidence in the persistence of this service under a changing climate requires knowledge on how extreme storms damage the platform and vegetation; however, a comprehensive, quantified understanding of salt marsh–wave interactions under extreme events is lacking. A unique experiment was conducted by transferring intact salt marsh to one of the world’s largest wave flumes, and subsequently exposing it to increasingly higher waves that reach up to 2 m significant wave height. We show that marsh substrates can persist with negligible erosion, despite cumulative wave exposure. By contrast, the vegetation was progressively damaged during continued wave exposure, gradually reducing vegetation-related wave attenuation. Results emphasize that vegetation was most effective in attenuating waves at low-energy marsh coasts (up to 1 m), where attenuation exceeded 10% (up to 50%), whereas attenuation at high-energy marsh coasts (wave height > 1 m) does not exceed 10%. Our global assessment supports the differentiation between low- and high-energetic conditions resulting from the flume experiment. Our results suggest that the marsh platform remains stable under extreme wave events and that substantial wave attenuation by marsh vegetation is limited to low-energy marsh coasts. Salt marsh platforms resist erosion under extreme waves, but vegetation damage reduces wave attenuation; substantial wave attenuation by vegetation is mainly limited to low-energy marsh coasts with waves below 1 m.

title: Zeolite-catalysed olefin carbonylation based on tuning spatial confinement
source: Nature
abstract: Carbonylation is an important process used to produce aldehydes, carboxylic acids and esters1-5 that is usually catalysed by homogeneous metal complexes with ligands and iodide promoters6-12. Koch has reported that protons of mineral acids can also catalyse carbonylation13. Previous studies have demonstrated that Brønsted acidic zeolites can act as a heterogeneous, Koch-type catalyst for carbonylation of alcohols and olefins, but the products in this case are limited to tertiary carboxylic acids14-18. Here we show that targeted use of spatial confinement in a zeolite together with a high CO/olefin ratio can help break this limitation. We report that, with FER zeolite and a CO/olefin ratio of 360, olefin carbonylation can produce primary and secondary carboxylic acids as the main products; ethylene carbonylation to propanoic acid (PA) is achieved with 80% selectivity over 100 h and propylene carbonylation to isobutyric acid (IBA) is achieved with 95% selectivity over 750 h. The propylene and ethylene carbonylation selectivities decrease to 61% and 57%, respectively, as the CO/olefin ratio decreases to 24 and 90, respectively. Experiments in combination with theoretical calculations suggest that T2-O5 in eight-membered ring (8-MR) cavities of FER zeolite are the primary active sites for ethylene carbonylation and T3-O1 in ten-membered rings (10-MRs) are the primary active sites for propylene carbonylation. Our findings open new directions for olefin carbonylation and provide critical insights into the prerequisites for developing new zeolite-based carbonylation processes.

title: Cold activates a BH2 metabolic network promoting longevity and proteostasis
source: Nature
abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    Moderately cold temperatures extend lifespan and promote health across species
                    1–3
                    , yet the molecular mechanisms underlying these benefits remain unclear. Here we define a metabolite-driven, multi-tissue signalling system that links cold temperature to enhanced longevity and proteostasis in
                    Caenorhabditis elegans
                    . Cold temperature upregulates the biopterin-synthesis enzyme CAT-4 (GCH1 in humans), increasing production of dihydrobiopterin (BH2), a transportable reservoir for the bioactive cofactor tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4). BH2 is produced in muscle and transported to distal tissues, including the intestine and neurons, where it is converted into BH4 by the salvage enzyme DHFR-1. BH4 functions as an essential cofactor for phenylalanine hydroxylase PAH-1, promoting tyrosine synthesis and extending lifespan. This BH2–BH4 axis also prevents disease-related protein aggregation and subsequent neuronal dysfunction during ageing. Importantly, increasing BH2 synthesis specifically in muscle is sufficient to promote longevity and suppress pathological protein aggregation in distal tissues, even at normal or elevated temperatures. In human cells, BH2 or tyrosine supplementation reduces aggregation of polyQ-expanded proteins associated with Huntington’s disease, as well as mutant variants of TDP-43 and FUS that cause amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Together, these findings identify BH2 as a cold-induced metabolite of which the synthesis, intertissue transport and conversion into bioactive BH4 preserve organism-wide proteostasis and extend lifespan.

title: WEE1 opposes APC/CCDH1 activity to promote S phase entry
source: Nature
abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    WEE1 phosphorylates and inhibits the activity of cyclin-dependent kinases to prevent mitotic entry and establish a G2 DNA damage checkpoint
                    1–3
                    . Consequently, WEE1 inhibitors have been developed to be synthetically lethal in
                    TP53-
                    mutated tumours that become reliant on this WEE1-mediated checkpoint, and such inhibitors are undergoing clinical trials. However, WEE1 inhibitors also have efficacy in
                    TP53-
                    wild-type tumours, and many trials have been terminated owing to high levels of toxic side effects, suggesting that WEE1 has unknown functions. Here we show that WEE1 promotes cell cycle re-entry from quiescence (G0) by opposing the activity of the E3 ubiquitin ligase, anaphase-promoting complex–cyclosome bound to CDH1 (APC/C
                    CDH1
                    ). WEE1 phosphorylates CDH1 (
                    FZR1
                    ) at key residues that mediate the interaction between CDH1 and APC/C. Cells with loss of function of WEE1 during G0/G1 have delayed S phase entry, impaired G1/S transition, abnormal S phase accumulation of cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor p21
                    Cip1/Kip1
                    and a p21-dependent G2 arrest. Reduced expression of APC/C
                    CDH1
                    or p21 renders cells more sensitive to acute WEE1 inhibition, and both pathways are downregulated in cells with acquired WEE1 inhibitor resistance. These results reveal a mechanism of cell cycle control that has implications for how WEE1 inhibitors should be used in the clinic.

title: A single archaeon couples long-chain fatty acid oxidation to methanogenesis
source: Nature
abstract: Anaerobic degradation of complex organic compounds to methane and carbon dioxide is common in the deep subsurface biosphere and has long been considered to require syntrophic cooperation, with methanogens confined to the terminal use of simple C1 and C2 substrates. Thermodynamic considerations, multi-omics analyses and microcosm experiments suggest that archaeal lineages are capable of methanogenic degradation of complex substrates1-6. However, experimental validation in pure culture was lacking. Here we report the isolation of a thermophilic archaeon, Methanoglobus dolicholipophagus AA-75, affiliated with Archaeoglobi, from a Chinese petroleum reservoir. Strain AA-75 not only converts methanol into methane, carbon dioxide and acetate, but also uses saturated fatty acids varying from C7:0 to C18:0 and unsaturated fatty acids including C16:1, C18:1 and C18:2 to produce methane. We term the latter lipotrophic methanogenesis, which integrates β-oxidation of fatty acids with the Wood-Ljungdahl pathway and the canonical methyl-tetrahydromethanopterin:coenzyme M methyltransferase and methyl-coenzyme M reductase complexes, together with an intracellular electron transfer system. A formaldehyde-methanol branch probably functions as an auxiliary route for C1 metabolism during methanogenesis. Methane produced from stearate is moderately 13C-enriched (δ13C-CH4 = -40.0‰ to -36.3‰), distinct from the strong 13C depletion characteristic of canonical methanogenic pathways. These findings demonstrate that methanogens can function as primary degraders of complex organic matter, challenging the classical syntrophic paradigm and calling for refinement of current models of carbon cycling in the deep subsurface biosphere.

title: An environmentally regulated dichotomy in cell lineages of the root
source: Nature
abstract: Plant development is highly plastic, with growth and architecture continuously shaped by environmental conditions. Roots, for instance, adjust their development to local water, nutrient and soil conditions. Despite this plasticity, individual root cell types are generally viewed as largely homogeneous populations that progress along a single developmental trajectory1. Here we show that rather than progressing along a single developmental trajectory, most Arabidopsis root cell lineage trajectories exhibit a stereotyped bifid topology, as revealed by single-cell RNA sequencing and spatial transcript mapping. One branch is characterized by a transcriptional program that is shared across multiple cell types and enriched for genes associated with environmental responses, including abscisic acid (ABA) signalling. This state occurs reproducibly in a subset of cells across multiple cell types, independent of developmental lineage, thereby revealing an additional layer of root cell identity. It is conserved across Arabidopsis ecotypes and persists despite major perturbations in developmental identity. Moreover, it is reduced in ABA-deficient and ABA-insensitive mutants and becomes more prevalent under water-deficit conditions. Together, these findings reveal an additional layer of root cell identity that is superimposed on developmental lineage and its prevalence is modulated by environmental conditions. These results uncover a previously unrecognized source of environment-associated transcriptional heterogeneity shared across root cell types. An environment-regulated state is identified across multiple cell types at the root tip, revealing a shared dichotomy between cells with and without this state.

title: CD51 delineates functionally distinct astrocyte subtypes in neural circuits
source: Nature
abstract: Astrocytes perform a diverse range of tasks that facilitate brain physiology, raising the possibility that these diverse astrocytic roles are enabled by functionally distinct subtypes1,2. Recent studies identified molecular diversity among astrocytes3; however, whether this molecular heterogeneity reflects specialized astrocyte subpopulations with distinct functions remains unclear. Here, on the basis of previous molecular and functional studies4, we generated a CD51-FLP mouse line that enables direct comparison of the functional properties between CD51+ and CD51− astrocyte subpopulations in neural circuits in vivo. We show that CD51+ and CD51− astrocytes have unique morphological, physiological and developmental properties in both the cortex and hippocampus. Functional studies demonstrate that CD51+ astrocytes selectively promote synapse formation in the developing cortex and circuit plasticity in the hippocampus. Mechanistically, we found that CD51+ astrocytes function through glypican 6 to promote synapse formation in the cortex, while CD51 itself drives circuit plasticity in the hippocampus. Applying these findings to brain injury, we found that CD51+ astrocytes promote functional recovery after stroke through enhanced synaptic remodelling. Taken together, our studies identify specialized astrocyte subpopulations that exhibit distinct functional properties in the developing, mature and injured brain. CD51+ astrocytes promote synapse formation in the developing cortex, circuit plasticity in the hippocampus and circuit remodelling after stroke.

title: Persistent neuronal stress signalling underlies Angelman syndrome phenotypes
source: Nature
abstract: Angelman syndrome is a severe neurodevelopmental disorder caused by the loss of UBE3A, a gene that encodes an E3 ubiquitin ligase1,2. The mechanisms that underlie Angelman syndrome are not well understood, and in particular, the link between UBE3A substrates and disease phenotypes remains uncertain3. Here, using gain- and loss-of-function mutations in UBE3A4,5 along with unbiased proteomics, we show that asparagine synthetase (ASNS) is a target of UBE3A. We find that ASNS protein abundance is increased in the brains of Ube3a-null mice and in human neurons6. Genetic correction of ASNS overabundance rescues microcephaly and many behavioural deficits. Detailed molecular analyses show that ASNS overabundance activates stress signalling and causes a global reduction in neuronal protein synthesis. Our results suggest that loss of UBE3A traps neurons in a state of persistent stress and stunts neuronal growth during developmentally sensitive periods. Moreover, our results indicate that targeting ASNS and the stress response could hold therapeutic potential in Angelman syndrome. Genetic and proteomic analyses in human neurons and mouse models of Angelman syndrome (AS) show that loss of the ubiquitin ligase UBE3A leads to an overabundance of asparagine synthetase, and that this is linked with many AS phenotypes.

title: GRP75-dependent SIMPA mediates inter-organellar quality control
source: Nature
abstract: Mitochondria are bound by a double membrane and are semiautonomous organelles, rendering them highly vulnerable to global and internal proteostatic stress1. Multiple surveillance mechanisms at proteostatic and inter-organellar levels have evolved to maintain mitochondrial integrity and cellular health2-7. However, the precise mechanisms by which proteostatic damage relays stress signals across organelles and how the quality surveillance machinery coordinates these functions remain unknown. Here we report that under proteostatic stress, damaged mitochondrial proteins are sequestered to form stress-induced mitochondrial protein aggregates (SIMPAs) that activate specific quality control mechanisms in a spatially confined manner without perturbing the mitochondrial network. Quantitative proteomic and correlative light-electron microscopy analysis revealed that SIMPA mediates inter-organellar communication via mitochondria-endoplasmic reticulum contact sites or mitochondrial-associated membranes. Mechanistically, GRP75 coordinates SIMPA biogenesis and focally activates endoplasmic reticulum unfolded protein response pathways via mitochondria-endoplasmic reticulum contact sites or mitochondrial-associated membranes for the targeted clearance of SIMPAs. Functionally, in both cellular and liver disease models, we found that a GRP75-dependent SIMPA signalling cascade attenuates mitochondrial stress and preserves mitochondrial integrity under proteotoxic stress. Overall, we show that SIMPAs, functioning as protein condensates, serve as a central cross-compartment communication hub for mitochondrial quality control, supporting cellular and organismal fitness.

title: How a new wave of science philanthropists can have the greatest impact
source: Nature
abstract: Tech entrepreneurs are bringing an engineer’s eye to research funding. They must be open about their findings to reap maximum benefit.

title: Programmable design of functional proteins from natural language
source: Nature
abstract: Programming biological function-designing bespoke proteins to perform specified molecular tasks-is a foundational goal of molecular engineering. However, current design models remain fundamentally limited1-3: they typically require either natural proteins as starting points for optimization or manual reformulation of functional goals as geometric and sequence-level constraints to guide candidate generation. Here we introduce Pinal, a 16-billion-parameter foundation model that designs candidate proteins from natural-language descriptions of desired function. Trained on 1.7 billion synthetically annotated protein-text pairs, Pinal links functional intent to protein sequence and structure. In computational evaluations, generated candidates combined high predicted foldability with functional-description alignment and sequence diversity, providing a basis for prioritizing experimentally testable designs. We applied Pinal to four distinct design tasks-a fluorescent protein, a polyethylene terephthalate hydrolase, an alcohol dehydrogenase and a metabolic H-protein-and experimentally observed the intended function in each case, including catalytic activity for both designed enzymes. Without iterative experimental optimization, a Pinal-designed H-protein increased product titre by 1.7-fold relative to the corresponding native Escherichia coli H-protein in a multi-enzyme CO2 fixation pathway. These findings support natural language as a high-level interface for candidate generation in protein design, enabling programmable exploration with reduced reliance on manually specified structural or sequence constraints.

title: Amazon carbon emissions driven by human actions amplified by droughts
source: Nature
abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    The Amazon carbon sink is weakening as deforestation
                    1–5
                    , rising tree mortality
                    6–8
                    and climate change disrupt the climatic conditions that sustain a humid tropical forest
                    9–11
                    . Forest loss reduces precipitation, increases temperatures and lengthens the dry season, driving higher carbon emissions
                    1–4,11,12
                    . Climate stress is stronger in more deforested regions, rendering forests progressively more flammable
                    1,9,13
                    . Large-scale climate events, such as El Niño, further amplify regional climate impacts
                    9,14–17
                    . Here we present an analysis of 15 years of Amazonian carbon fluxes derived from atmospheric CO
                    2
                    measurements. We determine a carbon balance of 0.32 ± 0.08 PgC yr
                    −1
                    , with fires acting as the dominant source (0.40 ± 0.07 PgC yr
                    −1
                    ) and forest uptake becoming increasingly unable to offset emissions. Furthermore, we investigate key drivers of the carbon emissions of Amazonia and identify three distinct year groups. Group 1 (2011–2014, 2017 and 2018) represents the role of the Amazon in the global carbon balance (0.11 ± 0.08 PgC yr
                    −1
                    ) during wetter years with low human activity, such as deforestation, biomass burning and degradation. Group 2 (2019–2022) represents Amazon carbon emissions (0.43 ± 0.13 PgC yr
                    −1
                    ) from human activities (mainly deforestation and degradation) during years with low climatic stress. Group 3 (2010, 2015, 2016, 2023 and 2024) has the highest carbon emissions (0.49 ± 0.07 PgC yr
                    −1
                    ) and comprises warm and dry years (high climate stress), such as El Niño and the warming of the Tropical North Atlantic Ocean, associated with biomass burning.

title: The proteome of Middle Pleistocene Xujiayao and common Denisovan morphology
source: Nature
abstract: The taxonomy and phylogeny of late Middle Pleistocene hominins in East Asia remain highly debated1. Xujiayao, a key representative assemblage with many fossils and a clear stratigraphy dating to around 199–138 thousand years ago, has been extensively studied, but its evolutionary position remains uncertain. Here, to clarify this, we analysed Xujiayao material through both palaeoproteomic analysis and morphological comparisons with other East Asian late Middle Pleistocene archaic Homo. Proteomic analysis of two specimens identified 18 endogenous proteins, and the Denisova-specific COL1A2-996 R>K mutation strongly supported their affiliation with the Denisovan lineage. Extended analysis identifies a set of shared morphological traits between Denisovan fossils (Xujiayao and Harbin) and other East Asian late Middle Pleistocene archaic Homo (such as Jinniushan, Dali and Hualongdong), indicating that they all belong to the Denisovan lineage. This analysis provides a comprehensive view of Denisovan features, showing both traits reminiscent of Homo erectus (such as a thick cranial vault) and those characteristic of modern humans (for example, a strongly arched temporal squama). They also share features with late Neanderthals, such as the structure of the temporal labyrinth and the presence of a suprainiac fossa. Notably, Denisovans are distinctive, with a low cranial profile with near-parallel lateral walls, a massive supraorbital torus, a flat zygomaxillary region and weak prognathism. Denisovans from the Xujiayao and other East Asian sites are morphologically distinctive, with a low cranial profile with near-parallel lateral walls, a massive supraorbital torus, a flat zygomaxillary region and weak prognathism.

title: Functional architecture of the human insula
source: Nature
abstract: The insular cortex has a central role in pain1,2, interoception3,4 and feelings5,6, yet its functional architecture and causal electrophysiological relationships among its subregions remain poorly understood. Here we combine intracranial electrical stimulation and task-based electroencephalography recordings with connectivity mapping within a cytoarchitectonic atlas of the human insula7-10 in 87 participants implanted with intracranial electrodes, and identify a quadripartite functional architecture comprising four distinct regions: (1) a dorsal-posterior region encoding somatotopically organized nociceptive/thermoceptive and somatosensory signals; (2) a ventral-posterior region with access to somatic information across multiple body parts; (3) a mid-anterior region associated with visceral sensations and anxiety states; and (4) an anterior-polar region, largely silent to direct stimulation, yet showing robust activation during salience detection and change of action mode. Critically, this anterior region, with its strong connections with the prefrontal cortex, including the anterior cingulate cortex, exerts strong and direct influence over other insular regions, while receiving less-strong indirect inputs from them, revealing an electrophysiological pathway for cognitive modulation of pain and bodily perception. Together, these findings define a functional architecture of the human insula that links cytoarchitecture to directed and asymmetric electrophysiological interactions, with mechanistic implications for cognitive modulation of pain and interoceptive experience.

title: Touch-sensing digital pixel fibre enables interactive garment GUI
source: Nature
abstract: Wearable computing promises to transform human interaction with information, yet conventional graphical user interfaces (GUIs) rely on planar, rigid displays incompatible with textiles, which are composed of one-dimensional fibres. Despite recent progress1,2 in flexible and fibre-based displays, bridging this fundamental dimensional mismatch remains challenging because existing approaches do not naturally provide the digitally addressable, high-throughput, information-rich interfaces required for interactive GUIs. Here we present a digital pixel fibre integrating addressable pixels, a common propagation-axis interconnection for scalable in-fibre circuitry and a coaxial sensing layer for fibre-level touch localization. Microelectronic components and a touch-gated resistive path system form a linear circuit that acts as both an interactive display backbone and a computational bus, while peripheral multimodal fibre sensors and actuators enable physiological, inertial, optical, and acoustic input and output. We integrate these fibres into the forearm portion of a garment sleeve to realize a GUI with a 96 × 54-pixel display, 30-frame-per-second refresh rate and 8-bit colour depth. It supports dynamic graphics, integrated audio-video playback, wireless data exchange and interactive computing functions, while maintaining the flexibility, washability, breathability and mechanical robustness of everyday textiles. By merging display, sensing and computation within a single fibre, this work establishes a scalable platform for intrinsically interactive textiles, opening pathways toward garments that operate as fully integrated computational systems.

title: Drought and disease trigger novel interactions among top predators
source: Nature
abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    Interactions among species are increasingly recognized as key determinants of climate change impacts on ecosystems
                    1–5
                    . However, we know little about how climatic perturbations affect interactions among top vertebrate predators. Here we show that, when an emergent disease caused the decline of shared prey (rabbits), after decades of neutral co-existence a mammalian carnivore (lynx) started to prey heavily on a top predatory raptor (kites). These predation bouts occurred exclusively under drought conditions and when lynx found rabbit remains under the raptor nests, consistent with the removal of a potential competitor. Drought-induced lynx predation depressed lifetime reproductive success and triggered territory abandonment and dispersal by the raptor, suggestive of a new arms race among predators. A reduction in raptor abundance was associated with an increase in an insectivorous bird (a small owl), showing that the new interaction had the potential to reach lower trophic levels. These results underline the importance of diet flexibility and mobility as important mediators of resilience to stressors. In the future, synergistic effects of multiple anthropogenic stressors may reshape the interactions and ecological roles of many apex predators, with potential cascading consequences for whole ecosystems. A key to forecasting the future impact of global change may reside in understanding how behavioural flexibility and interacting keystone species respond to interacting shocks.

title: Additive manufacturing of ultralong and architected single crystals
source: Nature
abstract: Single-crystal materials are indispensable for high-performance applications, yet their deployment remains constrained by conventional manufacturing techniques that depend on strict quasi-steady thermal conditions1. This requirement fundamentally conflicts with the intense cyclic thermal fluctuations inherent to additive manufacturing2, historically preventing the 3D printing of large or architected single crystals. Here we present a free-form additive manufacturing approach that resolves this contradiction by using delicately controlled alternating and pulsed heat inputs to govern and direct single-crystal growth. Using this method, we demonstrate the fabrication of metre-tall, centimetre-diameter single-crystal Ti-6Al-4V alongside, to our knowledge, the first single-crystal lattice structures containing complex zigzag ligaments, effectively eliminating theoretical size constraints for single-crystal components. The resulting bulk single-crystal Ti-6Al-4V exhibits an order-of-magnitude increase in creep resistance over standard grain-size scaling predictions, driven by the synergistic elimination of grain boundaries and an additive manufacturing-induced hierarchical α/β-architecture that regulates dislocation density, mobility and void evolution. Furthermore, we demonstrate the broad applicability of this technique by printing single crystals of hard-to-process refractory metals, including W, Mo, Nb and MoNb alloys. Our work introduces a large-scale method for single-crystal additive manufacturing, expanding the accessible materials library and enabling high-performance, complex geometries previously unattainable by classical methods.

title: Enzyme-embedded polyesters for accelerated biodegradation in the deep sea
source: Nature
abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    The accumulation of persistent plastics in the ocean is causing wide-ranging environmental problems
                    1–3
                    . Some commercially available compostable plastics
                    4–7
                    , developed to address these issues, degrade efficiently under industrial composting conditions; however, their degradation in marine environments, particularly in the deep sea, remains limited
                    8–10
                    . Here we demonstrate that thermally embedding enzymes into compostable polyesters (poly(butylene succinate) (PBS), poly(butylene succinate-
                    co
                    -adipate) (PBSA), poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL) and poly(butylene adipate-
                    co
                    -terephthalate) (PBAT)) significantly accelerates their degradation in both coastal and deep-sea environments from water depths of 2–6 m to 5,503 m. Enzyme-embedded polyesters achieved near-complete degradation at a deep-sea depth of 757 m within 5 months. Furthermore, moderate biodegradation of enzyme-embedded polyesters was observed under extreme conditions on deep-sea floors of 5,503 m. In coastal seawater, films embedded with trace amounts (0.1 wt%) of enzyme underwent rapid degradation. The mechanical properties of enzyme-embedded polyesters were similar to those of enzyme-free polyesters. Chemical analysis confirmed the formation of low-molecular-mass degradation products and biochemical oxygen demand measurements supported the mineralization of the enzyme-embedded polyesters. The enzyme-embedding strategy enables enhanced marine degradation of compostable polyesters and represents a potential solution to marine plastic pollution.

title: The anatomy of a personal health agent
source: Nature
abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    Large language models are enabling a new generation of health agents, yet their ability to address the diverse needs of individuals in everyday health settings remains underexplored
                    1,2
                    . Here we developed a comprehensive personal health agent that reasons over multimodal data from consumer wellness devices and medical records to provide personalized health support. Through analysis of web search and health forum queries, together with user-centred research involving end users and health experts, we identified four key user journeys: general health knowledge, personal data interpretation, wellness advice, and symptom assessment. These journeys informed three specialist sub-agents: (1) a data science agent that analyses longitudinal wearable and medical data, incorporating population-level statistics to contextualize numerical insights; (2) a health domain expert agent that integrates personal and contextual data with health knowledge to generate personalized insights; and (3) a health coach agent that synthesizes insights, supports multi-turn interaction and goal setting, applies specified psychological strategies and tracks progress. We integrated these capabilities in the personal health agent, an open-source multi-agent framework for dynamic, personalized health interactions. We evaluated the sub-agents and full system across 11 benchmark tasks using automated and human evaluation, with more than 7,000 annotations and 1,350 h of effort from health experts and end users. This represents the most comprehensive evaluation of a personal health agent thus far and provides a concrete foundation for improving access to high-quality personalized health support more broadly.

title: Solar vapor generation technologies: fundamentals, innovations and applications
source: Chemical Society Reviews
abstract: This Tutorial Review establishes a unified framework connecting the fundamentals of solar vapor generation with materials and structural design, providing guiding principles for efficient, scalable, and sustainable water production.

title: Recent applications of asymmetric hydrogenation in total synthesis of natural products and drugs
source: Chemical Society Reviews
abstract: This review focuses on recent advances of asymmetric hydrogenation in the strategic total synthesis of natural products and drug molecules, and outlines future perspectives for this field.

title: Octupole-driven spin torque switching of antiferromagnetic tunnel junctions
source: Nature
abstract: Magnetic tunnel junctions based on ferromagnets are canonical devices in spintronics, with wide-ranging applications in data storage, computing and sensing. They simultaneously exhibit mechanisms for electrical detection and control of magnetic order through the tunnelling magnetoresistance (TMR)1-5 and spin-transfer torque6-9 effects, respectively. It was long assumed that neither of these effects could be sizeable in all-antiferromagnetic tunnel junctions (AATJs), considering that they have no net magnetization. However, it was recently shown that AATJs based on chiral antiferromagnets do exhibit TMR due to their non-relativistic momentum-dependent spin polarization and cluster magnetic octupole moment, which are manifestations of their spin-split band structure10-13. However, the reciprocal effect, that is, the antiferromagnetic counterpart of spin-transfer torque, has been assumed non-existent due to the total electric current being spin-neutral. Here we report nanoscale AATJs that display this reciprocal effect, which we term octupole-driven spin-transfer torque (OTT). We demonstrate current-induced OTT switching of PtMn3|MgO|PtMn3 AATJs, with a TMR value of 363% at room temperature and switching current densities of the order of 10 MA cm-2. Our theoretical modelling explains the origin of OTT in terms of the imbalance between intra- and inter-sublattice spin currents across the AATJ, and, equivalently, in terms of the non-zero net cluster octupole polarization of each PtMn3 layer. This work establishes a new materials platform for antiferromagnetic spintronics and provides a pathway towards deeply scaled magnetic memory and room-temperature terahertz technologies.

title: Triboelectric DC generation via dielectric polarization coupling for self-powered IoT systems
source: Energy & Environmental Science
abstract: A contact-electrification-induced dielectric polarization mechanism enables unidirectional charge transfer for stable, low-crest-factor direct-current generation, thereby supporting robust self-powered operation of a multi-sensor IoT system.

abstract: Researcher and policy adviser who championed tests and treatments for genetic diseases.

title: Roll-to-Roll Fabrication of Large-Area Electrochromic WO3 Films via Slot-Die Coating and Intense Pulsed Light Processing
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Electrochromic tungsten oxide (WO3) films are promising candidates for flexible smart window applications. However, realizing large-area WO3-based electrochromic devices fabricated by low-temperature solution processing remains challenging. Here, we report a roll-to-roll (R2R)-compatible strategy for the fast fabrication of electrochromic WO3 films by synergistically combining an ultrafast intense pulsed light (IPL) process with trace Pt additives acting as light absorbers. Pt-incorporated WO3 (WO3-Pt) films were coated onto flexible substrates and subsequently treated within 10 ms using intense broadband irradiation from a xenon flash lamp. Structural, optical and chemical analyses indicate that the IPL process promotes the photothermal modification of WO3, while the Pt additive significantly enhances photothermal heating efficiency and electronic conductivity of the WO3 films. When integrated into electrochromic devices, the IPL-treated WO3-Pt (WO3-Pt-IPL) films exhibit high optical contrast, accelerated switching kinetics, and enhanced cycling stability compared to bare and IPL-treated WO3 films without Pt. The electrochromic device based on WO3-Pt-IPL film exhibited the highest optical contrast of 61.5% at 550 nm and a coloration efficiency (CE) of 139 cm2 C–1, whereas the devices based on bare WO3, WO3-Pt, and WO3-IPL films showed lower optical contrast values of 55.5%, 59.7%, and 59.3%, respectively, with CE values of around 80 cm2 C–1. In addition, the WO3-Pt-IPL device maintained nearly constant bleached and colored transmittance over 1500 cycles, demonstrating markedly improved cycling stability compared with the other device configurations. We further demonstrate large-area fabrication of WO3 films via R2R slot-die coating combined with IPL processing, achieving excellent spatial uniformity. This approach enables energy-efficient and scalable production of flexible metal oxide films and provides a feasible pathway for tuning charge transport and electrochromic properties in electrochromic materials.

title: Global emissions slow — but world hurtles towards 2 °C of warming
source: Nature
abstract: The United Nations’ latest climate report is a stark reminder that limiting warming to the safest levels is now likely out of reach.

title: Cooling water to near freezing breaks the activity–stability trade-off of water oxidation electrocatalysis
source: Nature Chemistry
abstract: Temperature is a fundamental parameter in reaction kinetics, typically accelerating rates according to the Arrhenius law. In catalytic systems, however, competing pathways often respond differently to temperature, allowing the selective promotion of desired reactions while suppressing undesired ones through temperature modulation. Here we show that regulating the temperature near the freezing point of water can resolve the activity-stability trade-off in the oxygen evolution reaction on manganese dioxide. Although lowering the temperature decreases water oxidation rates, catalyst degradation through permanganate formation is suppressed more effectively, extending catalyst lifetime. Counterintuitively, further cooling below 0 °C accelerates permanganate formation, yielding an optimum temperature near 0 °C that balances activity and stability. This anti-Arrhenius behaviour, arising from electrolyte supercooling, is a rare example of anomalous temperature-dependent electrocatalysis under subzero conditions. Our findings highlight temperature regulation as a viable strategy for enhancing catalytic lifetime, with implications for electrochemical systems operating in wintertime and in polar and extraterrestrial environments.

title: The right of way in Dublin
source: Nature Cities
abstract: At the front gate of Trinity College Dublin, trams, buses, taxis, bicycles and pedestrians compete for the same seconds of green. Xiaowen Tao reflects on how a city decides, signal by signal, who goes first and whose time is worth more, and argues that those decisions deserve to be debated as openly as any other public choice.

title: Institutional lock-in in urban building may constrain climate ambitions
source: Nature Cities
abstract: Cities are moving from climate pledges to delivery, yet construction rules still reward inherited routines. Using timber as an analytical lens, we highlight how institutional lock-in could delay low-carbon material transitions even as carbon caps and supply-chain scrutiny tighten.

title: De novo design of enantioselective artificial metalloenzyme photocatalysts
source: Nature
abstract: The ability to create protein scaffolds that impart enantioselectivity to simple, readily available metal catalysts could redefine the landscape of asymmetric catalysis. Artificial metalloenzymes (ArMs), hybrid catalysts that combine a synthetic metal cofactor with a protein scaffold, offer a potential means to achieve this goal, but scaffold discovery has remained constrained by trial-and-error approaches and the functional limits of extant proteins.1–5 This challenge is acute for metal polypyridine photocatalysts, which are widely used in visible-light chemistry but have not enabled highly enantioselective photocatalysis within protein scaffolds. In this study, we show that generative protein design6–8 can create de novo scaffolds that selectively bind these photocatalysts and that directed evolution converts the resulting artificial metalloenzymes into efficient, highly enantioselective photocatalysts9. The evolved proteins support diverse light-driven reactions, high catalyst turnover and catalyst recycling, and can function with commercially available racemic metal complexes. Spectroscopic studies show that the protein environment extends the photocatalyst excited-state lifetime and organizes substrate near the cofactor, altering energy transfer and controlling stereoselectivity. These findings establish de novo protein design as a route to functional scaffolds for synthetic metal complexes that lack natural protein partners and provide a strategy for combining protein design and evolution to control non-natural catalytic chemistry.

title: An AI tool improves weather forecasts up to a month ahead
source: Nature
abstract: An innovative artificial-intelligence application enhances weather forecasting in the difficult subseasonal range, providing accurate forecasts of precipitation, temperature and pressure 3–5 weeks in advance. The tool refines both physics- and AI-based weather models and improves the early prediction of extremes of heat, cold, rainfall and flooding. The tool boosts the ability of physics- and AI-based forecasting models to predict typical and extreme weather events.

abstract: Embedding enzymes that break down ester bonds into compostable polyesters enables rapid and complete biodegradation even in microbe-scarce environments. This method is effective in marine sites ranging from coastal sea water to the deep sea, and could therefore contribute towards solving the global plastic pollution problem. Polyesters containing ester-bond-breaking enzymes could help to reduce plastic pollution in marine environments.

abstract: A 450,000-year stalagmite record of rainfall in the Amazon Basin , combined with existing Asian records, shows that the global monsoon system has oscillated regularly, strengthening in one hemisphere while weakening in the other. However, during intervals of warmth and warming climate, monsoons in both hemispheres failed for millennia. The South American and Asian monsoons have both weakened during past periods of rapid warming.

title: Structural basis for protocadherin-1 recognition by New World hantaviruses
source: Nature
abstract: Hantaviruses are rodent-borne pathogens that cause severe human disease for which no approved therapeutics are available. New World hantaviruses, including Andes virus (ANDV), use the cell-surface receptor protocadherin-1 (PCDH1) to enter host cells1. However, the structural basis of this interaction remains unclear. Here we describe the structure of PCDH1 bound to the ANDV spike at near-atomic resolution. PCDH1 asymmetrically engages a deep central pocket formed by four Gn protomers in the spike, explaining why only intact viral particles or soluble tetramers recognize it. Mutagenesis identified three Gn loops that shape the receptor-binding site and afford the transfer of PCDH1 binding from New World to Old World glycoproteins. Structural and functional analyses of four neutralizing antibodies revealed that they block receptor binding through two distinct mechanisms—occluding access to the PCDH1-binding site or sterically preventing receptor engagement. Together, these findings define the structural determinants of hantavirus–receptor recognition, reveal how a virus can mask its receptor-binding site by recessing it in a surface depression and how antibodies can counter this strategy, and provide a framework for the design of antiviral therapeutics targeting the hantavirus spike. The structure of PCDH1 bound to the ANDV spike defines the structural determinants of hantavirus–receptor recognition.

title: A Pseudo-Icosahedral RhH2Au10 Superatom: Two Hydrogen Atoms Acting as Gold-Atom Equivalents and Modifiers
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract A hydrogen atom is known to act as a gold-atom-equivalent dopant in gold nanoclusters (AuNCs) by contributing to the valence electron count. To gain insights into the interaction of multiple H atoms with AuNCs, we herein synthesized a di-H-atom-doped NC, [RhH2Au10(dppp)5]3+ (RhH2Au10; dppp = 1,3-bis(diphenylphosphino)propane), by exposing [RhAu10(dppp)5]3+ (RhAu10) to H2 gas; RhAu10 was generated in situ via hydride (H–) abstraction from [RhHAu10(dppp)5]2+. Comprehensive characterization of RhH2Au10 by X-ray crystallography, NMR spectroscopy, and theoretical calculations revealed that the two H atoms occupy the two “missing” Au sites in the arachno-type RhAu10 core via dissociative adsorption of H2, forming a pseudo-icosahedral RhH2Au10 core. This core structure contrasts sharply with the previously reported di-H-atom-doped silver- or copper-based superatoms, in which the H atoms form an MH2 (M = Os, Ru, Rh) unit completely encapsulated within an icosahedral Ag12 or Cu12 shell.
