The RhH2Au10 core possesses an 8-electron closed-shell electronic configuration of (1S)2(1P)6, which is isoelectronic to the icosahedral RhAu12 superatom, thereby demonstrating the Au-atom equivalence of H atoms. Nevertheless, the two H atoms in the RhH2Au10 superatomic core act as structural modifiers compared to the RhAu12 superatom: (1) the degeneracy of the 1P orbitals is lifted by lowering the geometric symmetry, and (2) the HOMO–LUMO energy gap is expanded due to the reduced electronic confinement volume. This study demonstrates that multiple H atoms in a gold-based superatomic core not only behave as Au-atom equivalents but also serve as key components for modulating their fundamental properties.

title: Electrochemical Synthesis of Slaked Lime Utilizing a Diaphragm Flow Cell
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Slaked lime (Ca(OH)2) is one of the most widely utilized chemicals, with applications in diverse industries including construction, mining, water treatment, and chemical manufacturing. Currently, Ca(OH)2 is synthesized by coal-fired calcination of CaCO3 to make CaO, followed by exothermic hydration. Converting CaCO3 into Ca(OH)2 using electrochemically generated acid and base has attracted great interest because it could be powered by renewable electricity and would generate the CO2 byproduct in a pure form. Previous electrochemical Ca(OH)2 syntheses have incorporated the processing of calcium salts within the electrochemical cell to avoid acid–base recombination losses, but these cells have poor stability and high energy demand. Herein, we show that production of high-salinity acid and base solutions using a diaphragm flow cell (DFC) coupled with ex situ processing of CaCO3 substantially improves the efficiency of electrochemical Ca(OH)2 production. Using a closed loop with a simple KCl salt solution, we demonstrate the synthesis of >99% pure Ca(OH)2 for 0.088 to 0.10 kWh per mole at productive current densities of 158 to 334 mA cm–2.

title: Sugar-Based 1-Dimensional Metal–Organic Chalcogenolates with Hydration-Tunable Chiroptical Emission
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Chiral topology in semiconductors introduces a structural degree of freedom for tuning the chiroptical, excitonic, and spintronic behavior. In metal–organic chalcogenolates (MOChas) semiconductors, how ligand stereochemistry and supramolecular organization influence chiral topology, and thus optical and excitonic responses, remains poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate intrinsic circularly polarized luminescence (CPL) in sugar-based 1-dimensional MOChas, with structures solved via small-molecule serial femtosecond crystallography. These materials exhibit blue and green CPLs, arising from the chiral inorganic core. Despite the close chemical similarity between the glucose- and galactose-derived ligands, we observed dramatic differences in their inorganic structure. Silver glucosethiolate shows reversible hydration-driven photoluminescence switching with a hydration-linked emission energy. Labile water molecules in the glucose-based system correlate with a blueshift in excitonic emission. Our results suggest a new direction in the search for chirophotonic hybrid semiconductors, exploiting intrinsically chiral topologies and excitonic optical frequencies, which are sensitively modulated by ligand identity and supramolecular interactions.

title: Efficient Chemical Synthesis and Enzymatic Replication of 3′-Deoxyapionucleic Acid (ApioNA): An RNA-Selective XNA with Conformational Flexibility
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Xeno-nucleic acids (XNAs) have emerged as versatile platforms due to their sugar scaffolds that enable precise chemical tuning, leading to distinct classes ranging from fully compatible systems to orthogonal systems. However, sugar-modified XNAs capable of discriminating between RNA and DNA have remained elusive. In this work, we establish 3′-deoxyapionucleic acid (ApioNA) as a structurally flexible XNA with inherent RNA-selective hybridization properties. We achieved efficient production of ApioNA oligonucleotides through an efficient asymmetric synthesis of their building blocks and systematically characterized their properties. Thermal melting analyses demonstrate that ApioNA forms moderately stable duplexes with RNA while exhibiting weak pairing with DNA and negligible self-association. Quantum mechanical calculations reveal that the apiofuranose ring populates two low-energy puckering states, and the addition of an extra methylene group enhances backbone flexibility, thereby favoring A-form geometry for RNA pairing while requiring a higher-energy state to accommodate B-form DNA. Despite its weak affinity for DNA, ApioNA supports a complete enzymatic replication cycle using commercial Therminator and Bst 3.0 polymerases with approximately 98% fidelity and is processed by native E. coli machinery in vivo. This work fills the RNA-selective niche in the XNA functional landscape and establishes sugar puckering dynamics and backbone flexibility as key design principles for programming nucleic acid pairing specificity.

title: Contrasting Oxygen and Chlorine Evolution Selectivity in Tunnel and Layered MnO2 Electrocatalysts
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Controlling competing oxygen and chlorine evolution is a key challenge in chloride-containing electrolysis, particularly under neutral saline conditions relevant to seawater electrolysis. Here, two phase-pure MnO2 polymorphs with contrasting crystallographic frameworks, α-MnO2 and δ-MnO2, were synthesized through surfactant-free routes and evaluated under comparable conditions. Tetragonal α-MnO2 with a 2 × 2 tunnel framework preferentially promoted oxygen evolution, whereas layered δ-MnO2 favored chlorine evolution. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy revealed no detectable chlorine signal for α-MnO2 after chlorine evolution, while δ-MnO2 exhibited pronounced chloride-associated surface modification. Electron paramagnetic resonance spectroscopy and density functional theory calculations further revealed distinct defect characteristics and substantially different oxygen-vacancy formation tendencies between the two frameworks. These observations suggest that framework-dependent defect formation influences chloride-associated surface chemistry and contributes to the contrasting oxygen and chlorine evolution selectivity. Importantly, the selectivity trend was retained when the MnO2 phases were integrated onto iridium-ruthenium-based dimensionally stable anodes. These results demonstrate that contrasting crystallographic frameworks and their associated defect characteristics can markedly alter anodic selectivity and provide a structural basis for designing selective electrodes for chloride-containing electrochemical systems.

title: Dual-State Tumor-Activated RNA Delivery for Tumor-Selective and Precision Therapy
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract RNA therapeutics hold transformative potential for precision oncology; however, their systemic application remains constrained by a fundamental tradeoff between prolonged circulation stability and efficient intracellular activation. Conventional polyethylene glycol (PEG)-based carriers provide antifouling protection but lack tumor responsiveness, resulting in limited tumor accumulation and suboptimal gene expression. In this study, we developed a nanosystem, the dual-state tumor-activated RNA platform (D-STAR), which enables a dynamic transition from a stealth circulatory state to an activated transfection state through stepwise environmental alternation by recognizing a narrow pH window. At physiological pH, D-STAR maintains a negative surface potential to minimize nonspecific interactions and extend its blood circulation. Within the tumor microenvironment and endo-/lysosomal compartments, progressive protonation induces charge reversal and strengthens cationic activation, thereby enhancing tumor retention, cellular uptake, and cytoplasmic mRNA release. The systemic administration of D-STAR enabled tumor-selective mRNA expression with limited off-target organ distribution and markedly enhanced intratumoral reporter activity compared with PEG-based controls. The therapeutic delivery of human neutrophil elastase mRNA suppressed tumor growth and prolonged survival in a CT26 syngeneic model without systemic toxicity. Collectively, D-STAR establishes a dual-state adaptive RNA delivery framework that decouples systemic stability from activation potency, thereby offering a generalizable strategy for context-responsive precision RNA therapeutics.

title: Polarization Modulation in Core–Shell Halloysite Nanotubes@Sulfides for Broadband Electromagnetic Wave Absorption
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Polarization modulation is an effective approach for developing electromagnetic wave (EMW) absorbing materials. However, it is still a challenge to enhance the polarization performance of composites by adjusting the components. Herein, a series of core–shell halloysite nanotubes (HNTs)@sulfides are synthesized via one-step hydrothermal treatment. The sulfide-modified composites have excellent dielectric loss and polarization loss, resulting in favorable EMW absorption performance. Among them, HNTs@MoS2 has an effective absorption bandwidth (EAB) of up to 6.02 GHz at a thickness of 2.12 mm. This paper proposes a technical strategy for achieving polarization modulation to develop efficient EMW absorbing materials.

title: Muscle-Inspired Micro/Nanofiber Composites via Flow-Assigned Hierarchical Alignment
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Plastic accumulation and microplastic exposure have increased the demand for renewable lightweight materials. Lignocellulosic fibers are promising alternatives for acoustic diaphragms, paper-based packaging, and automotive interiors. However, their practical application is limited by the inherent trade-off between low density and mechanical performance, with most high-strength composites relying on densification or additional reinforcing phases that compromise lightweight characteristics. Here, inspired by the multiscale alignment of human muscle, we develop an oriented lignocellulose micro/nanofiber composite (O-LMU) through a flow-field-assisted assembly strategy. This approach enables the construction of a highly ordered multiscale fiber architecture coupled with optimized nanoscale interfaces. Multiscale simulations reveal that optimized interfacial interactions and hierarchical fiber alignment promote hydrogen-bond network reconstruction, mitigate stress concentration, and facilitate efficient load transfer within the fiber network. Therefore, O-LMU achieves a low density of 0.71 g·cm–3, a specific strength of 205 kN·m·kg–1, a tensile stiffness of 2245 kN·m–1, and a toughness of 394 J·m–2. Notably, O-LMU exhibits a specific strength that is 2.4 times that of the lignocellulosic nanofiber film. The material can be recycled by aqueous disintegration and biodegrades under natural soil conditions. This work establishes a structure-driven strategy for designing lightweight, strong, and sustainable lignocellulosic materials beyond conventional densification-based reinforcement approaches.

title: Controlled Edge-Mediated Photoelectrochemical Thinning and Patterning of Transition Metal Dichalcogenides
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) are widely investigated for electrochemical and photoelectrochemical energy conversion applications, yet the oxidation processes that govern their stability in reactive electrolytes remain poorly understood. Here, we systematically compare dark electrochemical and illuminated photoelectrochemical anodic etching and thinning of mechanically exfoliated MoS2, WS2, MoSe2, and WSe2 flakes as a function of applied potential, electrolyte pH, irradiance, and oxidation time. In the dark, oxidation initiates at defect-rich flake edges and produces lateral etching without appreciable basal-plane thinning. The oxidation peak potentials exhibit significantly different pH dependences for sulfide- and selenide-based TMDs, revealing chalcogen-dependent oxidation chemistry and kinetics. Under illumination, an additional oxidation regime emerges at lower anodic potentials, in which multilayer n-type MoS2, WS2, and MoSe2 undergo vertical thinning with minimal lateral etching, whereas no thinning is observed for p-type WSe2. This observation, together with strong suppression of thinning by sacrificial hole acceptors, indicates that photogenerated holes accumulated in the upper layers of n-type TMDs drive a photoelectrochemical self-oxidation process. Tuning the bias, irradiance, and oxidation time enables controlled conversion of initially nonuniform multilayer flakes into homogeneous few-layer structures, while focused laser excitation yields spatially localized thinning and patterning. In addition to elucidating stability windows and oxidation mechanisms of TMD photoelectrodes, these results provide a versatile strategy for controllably tuning the thickness and morphology of layered semiconductors.

title: Advanced Thermoelectric Power Modules Employing n -Type Ag2Se Synthesized via a Sustainable Route
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Thermoelectric (TE) Ag2Se was synthesized via an energy-efficient, solution-based chemical synthesis route with microwave-assisted heating and compacted by sustainable cold pressing. Structural and TE transport property analyses confirmed a highly crystalline microstructure that promotes high electrical conductivity, a large Seebeck coefficient, and low thermal conductivity, yielding a peak TE figure of merit (ZT) of ∼0.85 at room temperature. To evaluate device-level performance, Ag2Se was employed as the n-type TE leg in modules paired with Sb1.5Bi0.5Te3 (ZT ∼1.1 at 325 K) as the complementary p-type TE leg. Both rigid and flexible modules, each containing 58 thermocouple pairs, were fabricated and benchmarked against a commercial TEC1-12706 module. The rigid module exhibited more than four times the maximum power output of the commercial reference, highlighting the promise of Ag2Se for low-temperature TE power applications. Cooling performance tests demonstrated the critical influence of electrical configuration. Series-connected rigid modules achieved the lowest cold-side temperatures at lower input power, reaching ∼2 °C at 18 W, comparable to or exceeding the cooling performance of the commercial device. In contrast, parallel-connected modules exhibited stronger initial cooling but were hindered by excessive current draw, Joule heating, and thermal instability, preventing stable saturation. Increasing input power would enhance cooling performance until saturation limits were reached. These results emphasize the importance of module architecture and thermal management for optimizing TE device performance. Overall, this work establishes Ag2Se as a promising alternative to conventional Bi-Sb-Te-based n-type materials, demonstrating versatility in both rigid and flexible TE modules for energy harvesting and cooling technologies.

title: Reprotonation Kinetics Engineering of Aramid Nanofiber Hydrogel Electrolytes for Aqueous Zinc-Ion Batteries
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Aqueous zinc-ion batteries are promising next-generation energy-storage systems owing to their intrinsic safety and cost-effectiveness. However, dendrite formation and parasitic reactions at Zn metal anodes limit long-term cycling stability. Here, aramid nanofiber (ANF) hydrogel electrolytes are engineered by controlling the acid identity and solution pH during reprotonation. These variables regulate reprotonation kinetics, thereby shaping hydrogen-bond formation, molecular ordering, and the through-thickness morphology of the ANF network. The selected ANF hydrogel electrolyte exhibits a Young’s modulus of 1.1 MPa while maintaining an ionic conductivity of 30.8 mS cm–1. Its mechanically robust and ionically conductive network promotes compact Zn deposition and resists dendrite penetration. Consequently, Zn||Zn symmetric cells sustain stable plating/stripping for over 2000 h at 1.0 mA cm–2 with an areal capacity of 1.0 mAh cm–2. Compared with conventional glass-fiber-based cells, Zn||hydrated vanadium oxide full cells also exhibit improved high-rate capacity retention and retain over 88% of their initial capacity after 2000 cycles at 1.0 A g–1. These findings establish reprotonation kinetics as a practical design parameter for balancing mechanical robustness, ion transport, and interfacial stability in hydrogel electrolytes for durable aqueous zinc-ion batteries.

title: Polymerization-Pathway-Dependent Zwitterionic Hydrogels for Time-Gated Information Encryption and Irreversible Optical Erasure
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Chameleon-like adaptive coloration inspires dynamic information camouflage, yet translating temporally programmable optical behavior into synthetic soft materials remains challenging. Here, we develop a zwitterionic pVS hydrogel for time-gated information encryption, decryption, and irreversible optical erasure. The system uses the established alkali-responsive fluorescence of VPES-derived units as the optical basis, while the SBMA-rich zwitterionic network suppresses swelling and preserves pattern fidelity. Spatially separated UV- and thermally initiated polymerization pathways generate domains with distinct initial emission states and alkaline-response trajectories within the hydrogel, allowing polymerization history to function as an intrinsic optical key. Quantitative kinetic analysis reveals progressive fluorescence convergence between the UV- and thermally initiated domains, with the red-emission contrast decreasing from 0.667 to 0.012 during prolonged alkaline treatment and preventing subsequent recovery of QR-code readability after acid treatment. This convergence establishes an operational time window for information security: short alkaline exposure produces a recoverable encrypted state, whereas excessive exposure permanently eliminates the optical contrast required for QR-code recognition, resulting in irreversible information self-destruction. This work provides a kinetically controlled hydrogel strategy for transient information protection and time-limited optical authentication.

title: Wet-Adhesive Hydrogel Patch for Sustained Oral Ulcer Treatment
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Oral ulcers are a common mucosal disorder that causes persistent pain and significantly impairs quality of life for patients. Current therapeutic approaches, including sprays and commercial patches, provide only temporary relief, as the complex, dynamic, and moist oral environment hinders prolonged retention and drug efficacy. Here, we report the rational design of a multifunctional hydrogel adhesive that integrates poly(acrylic acid) (PAA) for hydrogen bonding, polyamidoamine-epichlorohydrin (PAE) for electrostatic interactions with mucosal surfaces, and poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA) for swelling resistance. The resulting hydrogel exhibits an instant wet tissue adhesion strength of ∼40 kPa and enhances adhesion after prolonged immersion in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS). Remarkably, it retains high adhesion strength under extreme conditions, such as hypertonic and strongly acidic environments. When loaded with dexamethasone acetate, the hydrogel enables controlled drug release, significantly improving therapeutic outcomes in a rat oral ulcer model. By ensuring prolonged retention and effective drug delivery, this hydrogel patch offers a promising strategy for enhancing oral ulcer treatment.

title: Programming hot-carrier dynamics in gold nanoclusters for high-gain photodetectors
source: Chem
abstract: Gold nanoclusters have long been limited in optoelectronic applications by sub-picosecond hot-carrier cooling. Here, electron-donating ligands spatially separate the frontier orbitals of Au22 nanoclusters, extending hot-carrier lifetime to nanoseconds and enabling high-performance, stable photodetectors. This work establishes ligand engineering as a general strategy to tune excited-state dynamics in metal nanoclusters, offering chemists a new materials design route for next-generation optoelectronics beyond conventional semiconductors.

title: Biomembrane-Camouflaged Stents: Promising Strategies for Advanced Coronary Interventions
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Coronary stent implantation remains a cornerstone therapy for coronary artery disease, yet current stent technologies continue to face limitations including acute and late thrombosis, delayed re-endothelialization, chronic inflammation, and in-stent restenosis. These complications largely arise from the nonphysiological interface between the implanted device and the injured vascular microenvironment. Biomembrane-camouflaged stents have recently emerged as a promising strategy to engineer biologically instructive blood-contacting surfaces by integrating natural or artificial membrane systems onto stent platforms. In this review, we summarize recent advances in three major biomembrane-based strategies for coronary stent functionalization: cell membrane-camouflaged stents, liposome-camouflaged stents, and exosome-camouflaged stents. Biomimetic cell membrane coatings retain native bioactive signals that collectively facilitate immune evasion, thromboresistance, and vascular healing. Liposome-based coatings are tunable artificial biomembrane reservoirs for the localized delivery of anticoagulants, anti-inflammatories, nitric oxide releasers, antiproliferatives, and gene therapies. Exosome-functionalized stents further enable bioactive intercellular communication by transferring endogenous regulatory cargos that modulate endothelial regeneration, macrophage polarization, smooth muscle cell phenotype, oxidative stress, and neointimal remodeling. We further discuss fabrication approaches, biological mechanisms, preclinical evidence, translational barriers, and future design principles for these platforms. Although challenges remain in coating durability, sterilization, long-term storage, manufacturing reproducibility, and clinical validation, biomembrane-camouflaged stents represent a compelling direction for next-generation coronary intervention by transforming conventional stents from passive mechanical scaffolds into active regulators of vascular repair.

title: Iron Site Evolution in Fe-MFI Zeolite under Thermal Treatment: Spectroscopic Insights and Acetone Vapor Interactions
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Iron-containing MFI zeolites (Fe-MFI) and purely siliceous MFI were compared to assess the structural and electronic effects of iron incorporation. Powder X-ray diffraction confirms that the MFI framework is preserved after Fe introduction during synthesis. UV–vis and 57Fe Mössbauer spectroscopy show that iron is mainly present as Fe3+ in distorted [5]/[6]-coordinated and octahedral environments. In the as-synthesized material, Fe3+ accounts for ∼88% of the total iron, accompanied by a minor Fe2+ fraction (13%). After calcination, Fe2+ is fully oxidized to Fe3+ and redistributed nearly equally between distorted and octahedral sites. Nitrogen physisorption indicates a moderate loss of microporosity due to the partial pore occupation by FeOx species. Overall, Fe incorporation generates dispersed Fe3+ centers and small extra-framework FeOx species that subtly modify the structural and electronic properties of the MFI zeolite. These powders were incorporated into a membrane for acetone vapor detection, the Fe-MFI membrane showing a stronger and more distinct response to acetone exposure than the pure MFI membrane. In summary, this study establishes Fe-MFI membranes as promising active materials for acetone vapor interaction, providing a robust proof-of-concept for future gas-sensing applications. The key novelty of this work is the direct correlation between the calcination-induced redistribution of iron sites and the resulting vapor-sensing performance of the membrane.

title: Hierarchical Lead-Free Cs–Cu–I Multilayers Fabricated by Vacuum Molten Salt Deposition for Hydrochromic and Spectrally Multiplexed Optical Encryption
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Optical security labels are the front line of product authentication, yet mainstream photoluminescent tags emit a static, single-color signal that is easily replicated. Lead-free ternary copper halides of the Cs–Cu–I system combine nontoxicity and air stability with bright luminescence arising from self-trapped excitons. In solution processing, the lack of solvent orthogonality makes it difficult to stack CsCu2I3 and Cs3Cu2I5 layers within a single device. Here, we adapt the molten salt evaporation concept, previously developed for lead-halide perovskite photovoltaics, to the Cs–Cu–I system through a vacuum molten salt deposition strategy. Premixed CsI and CuI form a homogeneous molten source that mitigates the disparate volatilities of the two precursors and enables compositionally coupled evaporation. Phase-selective X-ray diffraction, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, and optical characterization confirm that the 1:2 and 3:2 sources yield the targeted one-dimensional (1D) CsCu2I3 and 0D Cs3Cu2I5 films, respectively. Because the process is solvent-free, the two phases can be deposited sequentially between transparent PDMS spacers to form an encapsulated PDMS/CsCu2I3/PDMS/Cs3Cu2I5/PDMS core, and adding a spatially patterned, unencapsulated Cs3Cu2I5 dynamic layer on top yields an integrated label that combines three independent security primitives. First, macroscopic transparency provides physical stealth, revealing nothing to the naked eye. Second, spectral gating with 325 nm excitation and a 510 nm long-pass filter unmasks the yellow CsCu2I3 pattern beneath the intense blue Cs3Cu2I5 emission. Third, moisture triggers a reversible 0D-to-1D phase conversion of the dynamic layer that executes a localized bit-flip in the optical code. A standalone unencapsulated Cs3Cu2I5 film and the integrated label remain stable for 200 days in ambient air, the dynamic layer withstands 20 hydration–dehydration cycles, and the encapsulated core withstands 20 days of water immersion. By combining solvent-free, phase-selective deposition with multistimulus optical encoding, this work provides a lead-free multilayer platform for optical encryption.

title: Robust Anomalous Hall Effect in Epitaxial Cubic D03-Fe3Ge Nanoplates Grown via Chemical Vapor Deposition
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Iron-based ferromagnetic materials have emerged as a promising system for spintronics due to their high Curie temperatures and the significant anomalous Hall effect (AHE) driven by Berry curvature. While there have been investigations into the epitaxial growth of nonlayered iron-based ferromagnetic materials, the realization of high-quality single crystal thin films continues to be a formidable obstacle. Meanwhile, issues such as grain boundary scattering further hinder their characterization and application. Here, we report the first chemical vapor deposition synthesis of single-crystalline cubic D03-Fe3Ge nanoplates. This compound represents a substantial departure from the conventional hexagonal phases typically observed in the Fe–Ge system. Structural characterizations confirm the cubic lattice and the stoichiometric purity of the crystals. Structural analysis identifies a strong epitaxial effect, resulting in a giant compressive strain of ∼4.16% at the interface that relaxes gradually toward the surface. The second-harmonic generation signals might further reveal that such interfacial strain disrupted the inherent centrosymmetry of the cubic phase. Superconducting quantum interference device magnetometry shows robust room-temperature ferromagnetism and clear magnetic anisotropy. Magneto-transport measurements reveal a robust AHE that remains stable at temperatures far exceeding the room temperature. The scaling observed between the anomalous Hall resistance and longitudinal resistance strongly suggests that this effect is dominated by the intrinsic Berry curvature mechanism. Furthermore, density functional theory calculations reveal that the huge epitaxial strain induces band reconstructions and creates dense spin–orbit coupling gaps near the Fermi level, effectively doubling the anomalous Hall conductivity to match our experimental observations.

title: NIR-Activated ROS/NO Cascade Nanocomposite Rewires Bacterial Redox Defense for Synergistic Eradication of Pseudomonas aeruginosa Wound Infection
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Pseudomonas aeruginosa wound infections remain difficult to eradicate because biofilm formation and bacterial redox-adaptive defenses weaken antibacterial efficacy and delay tissue repair. In this study, we reported a near-infrared (NIR)-activated reactive oxygen species (ROS)/ nitric oxide (NO) cascade nanocomposite, UCeSi-L@CA, designed to amplify oxidative/nitrosative antibacterial stress while promoting infected wound healing. UCeSi-L@CA was constructed from Ce6-loaded mesoporous silica-coated upconversion nanoparticles, with L-arginine conjugated through surface carboxyl groups and cinnamaldehyde loaded into the mesopores. Upon NIR irradiation, upconversion nanoparticles activated Ce6 to generate abundant ROS. Cinnamaldehyde exerted direct antibacterial activity and inhibited glutathione-mediated ROS scavenging, thereby sustaining ROS accumulation and weakening bacterial antioxidant defense. The accumulated ROS further triggered NO production from L-arginine, establishing a ROS/NO cascade in which ROS and NO cooperatively damaged bacterial membranes, enhanced lipid peroxidation, and induced efficient bacterial killing. Beyond antibacterial activity, NO also contributed to infected tissue repair. In vitro, UCeSi-L@CA + NIR showed excellent killing against planktonic P. aeruginosa, effectively inhibited biofilm formation, eradicated bacteria within established biofilms, and suppressed biofilm regrowth. In the P. aeruginosa-infected wound model, UCeSi-L@CA + NIR markedly reduced local bacterial burden, attenuated infection-associated inflammation, accelerated wound closure, and promoted tissue repair, with favorable biocompatibility in vitro and in vivo. This nanocomposite presents a non-antibiotic nanotherapeutic strategy integrating NIR-triggered ROS generation, cinnamaldehyde-mediated GSH-defense inhibition, and L-arginine-derived NO release for treating refractory biofilm-associated wound infections.

title: Direct Regeneration of Spent Graphite Electrodes Using an Organic Solvent-Free Approach: Evaluation of Aqueous- and Rapid Thermal Processing-Assisted Black Mass Delamination
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Sustainable recycling of graphite anodes is critical for enabling closed-loop lithium-ion battery manufacturing, yet most direct recycling methods rely on organic solvents and corrosive acid treatments that increase costs and environmental impacts. Herein, we evaluate an organic solvent-free, direct recycling strategy that combines aqueous graphite recovery with boric acid-assisted regeneration. Water-based delamination of graphite black mass was investigated using two representative commercial end-of-life graphite anodes and a commercially manufactured uncycled graphite anode. The effectiveness of aqueous separation of the black mass from the Cu current collector was investigated along with rapid thermal processing (RTP), which has been proposed to improve graphite recovery through binder degradation. Both methods resulted in effective graphite recovery despite impurities originating from ceramic-coated separators, Ti-containing additives, and current collector corrosion. However, delamination of RTP-treated spent anodes was more difficult than pristine anodes, requiring pre-RTP washing and ultrasonication for efficient graphite recovery. Boric acid treatment followed by calcination at 1050 °C increased the degree of graphitization for all spent graphite samples while removing residual surface species and trapped lithium. Electrochemical testing showed that the regenerated graphite largely recovered its capacity and electrochemical activity, although residual metallic impurities may limit long-term cycling stability. Overall, aqueous delamination combined with boric acid-assisted regeneration provides an effective and more sustainable route for graphite recycling by eliminating organic solvents and strong mineral acids while preserving favorable structural and electrochemical properties. This process offers a promising pathway for scalable, environmentally responsible recovery of graphite from end-of-life lithium-ion batteries.

title: Hydrophilic Zinc Metal-Organic Frameworks with Optimized Lewis Acid Centers for Enhanced Photocatalytic Performance
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Water-stable metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) have emerged as promising porous materials for addressing water pollution challenges, owing to their tailorable structures and unique active sites. However, the regulatory role of metal centers with fully or partially filled d orbitals in interfacial behaviors during advanced oxidation processes remains insufficiently understood, posing a critical barrier to the development of efficient decontamination systems. In this study, we rationally designed and fabricated a series of MOF materials featuring ordered π-conjugated skeletons. These MOFs were constructed using 2-aminoterephthalic acid as the ligand, incorporating diverse metal nodes (Zn, Ti, and Co), and engineering hydrophilic or hydrophobic channels. The tetracycline (TC) degradation efficiencies of these MOFs under visible-light irradiation were systematically compared. By correlating the degradation results with structural characteristics elucidated via X-ray diffraction (XRD), Brunauer-Emmett-Teller (BET) surface area analysis, and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), combined with photoelectrochemical measurements, the influence of different metal centers on charge separation efficiency was comprehensively evaluated. The findings reveal that the Zn-MOF exhibits exceptional photocatalytic performance, which originates from the closed-shell d10 electronic configuration of Zn2+. This unique electronic structure confines electrons within the organic linker, effectively suppressing the recombination of photogenerated electron–hole pairs. Furthermore, the incorporation of Zn2+ centers prolongs the lifetime of photoexcited electrons and optimizes the ligand-to-metal charge transfer (LMCT) process, thereby significantly enhancing photocatalytic activity. Radical trapping experiments identified superoxide radicals (•O2−), photogenerated electrons (e−), and holes (h+) as the dominant reactive species involved in the TC degradation process. This work highlights the potential of water-stable MOFs with suppressed charge recombination for applications in various photochemical processes beyond water treatment.

title: La Doping Imparts Bifunctional Interfacial Catalysis for Dehydrolactonization of 1,6-Hexanediol
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The dehydrolactonization of 1,6-hexanediol (1,6-HDO) to ε-caprolactone (ε-CL) requires a catalyst capable of cooperatively catalyzing two distinct half-reactions, namely dehydrogenation and cyclization. However, conventional catalysts lack the electronically asymmetric sites needed to drive both steps efficiently. Herein, a bifunctional Cu+–Ov–Ce3+ interfacial frustrated Lewis pair (FLP) is constructed by loading Cu onto La doping CeO2. La doping introduces additional oxygen vacancies (Ov) and Ce3+ species, thereby enriching the Ov–Ce3+ sites. Systematic characterizations (XPS, EPR, XAS, TPD, in situ FTIR) combined with DFT calculations reveal that Cu+ sites are responsible for α-H elimination to form 6-hydroxyhexanal (6-HA), whereas the cyclization reaction is driven by the FLP composed of Ov–Ce3+ and adjacent lattice oxygen. La incorporation lowers the energy barrier and enhances FLP formation. Under optimized conditions (3 wt % La, 280 °C, weight hourly space velocity of 1.5 h–1), a ε-CL yield of 61.17% is achieved with good stability over 120 h. From these findings, the interfacial bifunctional mechanism is clearly elucidated, and a defect engineering strategy for decoupling interfacial components is demonstrated, providing a rational approach to the design of multifunctional catalysts for tandem reactions.

title: Molecular Functionalization Tunes Twist Angles of MoS2 Moiré Superlattices for Surface-Enhanced Raman Scattering
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract In the quest for surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (SERS) substrates without noble metals, transition-metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) have emerged as an important class of alternatives. In this regard, molybdenum disulfide (MoS2)-based SERS substrates have been extensively studied; however, their moiré superlattices (with controlled twist angles) could be potent candidates for significant signal enhancement. Here, we employed a molecular functionalization method using 4-aminothiophenol (4-ATP) as a linker to tune the twist angles of MoS2 moiré superlattices. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and Raman spectroscopy experiments confirmed the formation of moiré patterns in 4-ATP functionalized MoS2 (4ATP-MoS2), with reduced twist angles in contrast to pristine MoS2 superlattices. Furthermore, we used 4ATP-MoS2 moiré superlattices as SERS substrates to probe molecules, such as rhodamine 6G, rhodamine B, methylene blue, and crystal violet. We observed significant enhancement of Raman signal intensity (on the order of 105) for all the molecules. Interestingly, pristine MoS2 did not show any significant enhancements of the SERS signals. We attribute the enhancement to the moiré interface-induced charge transfer from MoS2 to the probe molecules through 4-ATP, thereby increasing the Raman signals. This strategy could open possibilities to design moiré superlattices for improved SERS substrates and light–matter interactions.

title: Layer-Distortion Engineering of Acridinium-Based Covalent Organic Frameworks Enables Efficient Photoredox Transformations of Alcohols
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Planar two-dimensional (2D) covalent organic frameworks (COFs) often suffer from severe interlayer π–π stacking, which promotes excitonic recombination, restricts access to active sites, and compromises photocatalytic efficiency. Here we report a layer-distortion engineering strategy to construct wavy acridinium-based COFs, Mes-Acr-TAPB and Mes-Acr-TAPP, by introducing structural distortion into otherwise planar layered frameworks. The resulting wavy framework efficiently suppresses interlayer π–π stacking, enlarges interlayer spacing, modulates molecular packing, pore environment, and improves accessibility to photoactive acridinium sites. Compared with the planar analog Dur-Acr-TAPB, Mes-Acr-TAPB exhibits enhanced exciton dissociation along with substrate absorption, more efficient charge separation, and superior photocatalytic activity. As a heterogeneous photoredox catalyst, Mes-Acr-TAPB enables diverse alcohol transformations under mild conditions, including β-scission radical functionalization, ring contraction/expansion, and skeletal transposition. Mes-Acr-TAPB shows broad functional-group tolerance and supports late-stage structural modification of complex natural products, highlighting its synthetic utility. This work establishes layer-distortion as an effective design principle for mitigating interlayer stacking in 2D COFs and advancing high-performance COF photocatalysts for sustainable organic synthesis.

title: Energy Deposition Timescales Controls Chemistry in Pulsed Methane Plasmas
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Nonoxidative methane conversion offers a promising route for the coproduction of hydrogen and value-added hydrocarbons without CO2 emissions. Among emerging approaches, pulsed plasmas can provide potential advantages by enabling high energy deposition, rapid quenching, and generation of active nonthermal species. This work systematically investigates how pulsed energy deposition from nanosecond-to-millisecond time scales (10 to 50 mJ/pulse) influences methane plasma characteristics (electron density and gas temperature), reaction mechanisms, conversion, and energy efficiency. Nanosecond discharges produced the highest overall C2 selectivity (>70%), with up to 20% for C2H4; in this regime, methane dissociation proceeded through both electron-impact and thermal dissociation, whereas longer pulses were predominantly thermal. Pulsed plasma conversion was similar to thermal arcs (∼377 kJ/mol CH4) and specific energy requirements to produce C2H2 and H2 were 15 kWh/kg and 40 kWh/kg, respectively, in 100 μs long discharges. The product distribution was largely determined by thermal processes involving dehydrogenation reactions (Kassel’s reaction scheme). High gas temperatures preferentially favored C2H2 formation over C2H4, and C2H4 selectivity decreased with increasing pulse width. Overall, these results demonstrate that pulse width and energy can be used to tailor hydrocarbon selectivity and can help design pulsed plasma systems for efficient production of value-added hydrocarbons and hydrogen.

title: Enhancing Proton Conductivity in the Ce0.9Gd0.1O2–δ Electrolyte for Low-Temperature SOFCs via Surface Doping with a Cobalt Oxide Redox Mediator
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Developing oxide electrolytes with high ionic conductivity (∼0.1 S cm–1) at temperatures below 600 °C is essential for next-generation solid oxide fuel cells. However, current electrolyte materials rarely meet this benchmark, primarily because of limitations inherent in bulk doping and high-temperature sintering. To overcome this challenge, we demonstrate a surface engineering strategy that involves controlled cobalt doping onto the acid-etched surface of gadolinium-doped ceria (Ce0.9Gd0.1O2–δ, GDC), thereby constructing a Co3+/Co2+ redox mediator. The 3 mol% cobalt-surface-doped GDC (GDC-Co3) electrolyte exhibits optimal ionic transport behavior, achieving an ionic conductivity of 0.153 S cm–1 at 500 °C and a 30% improvement over pristine GDC (0.118 S cm–1), while simultaneously reducing the activation energy from 0.64 eV to 0.36 eV. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) and multi-wavelength Raman spectroscopy reveal that Co2+/Co3+ redox pairs are introduced onto the surfaces of GDC particles through doping with different Co(II)/GDC molar ratios. The formation of a Schottky junction, as evidenced by a rectifying effect, effectively prevents electron leakage across the electrolyte. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), combined with distribution of relaxation times (DRT) analysis, indicates that ionic conductivity is strongly correlated with electronic conductivity. These results collectively support a mechanism where surface-localized Co2+/Co3+ redox pairs act as mediators for the Ce4+/Ce3+ couples in GDC, establishing favorable surface pathways for proton transport via an alternating interstitial proton-hydrogen hopping process. The accompanying reduction in electrode polarization resistance suggests that accelerated interfacial reaction kinetics may also contribute to the improved cell performance, alongside enhanced proton transport. This work presents an innovative surface engineering approach that significantly enhances proton transport in fluorite oxide materials, with important implications for low-temperature solid oxide electrochemical devices.

title: Crossover from Asymmetric to Symmetric Electrowetting Linked to Double-Layer Restructuring
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Voltage-controlled wetting at solid–liquid interfaces is central to the performance of a range of electrochemical and microfluidic technologies, yet the molecular basis of polarity-dependent electrowetting remains unresolved. Classical electrocapillarity predicts a symmetric dependence of contact angle on applied potential, but experiments and simulations frequently exhibit pronounced asymmetry. Here, combining electrowetting measurements with atomistic simulations, we show that asymmetric wetting at aqueous carbon interfaces arises from the structure of the electrical double layer. By investigating aqueous KF and LiCl electrolytes at graphitic interfaces across lower concentration and water-in-salt regimes, we identify a crossover from strongly asymmetric electrowetting at lower concentration to a symmetric response at high concentration for KF, while LiCl retains a pronounced asymmetry. This transition is accompanied by corresponding changes in the solid–liquid interfacial tension, demonstrating that polarity-dependent wetting can arise from voltage-dependent molecular restructuring of the interfacial liquid, which modifies the interfacial thermodynamics, without invoking faradaic processes. We introduce interfacial connectivity, defined by the network of intermolecular interactions within the first adsorption layer, as a molecular descriptor linking double-layer structure to macroscopic wetting behavior. These results demonstrate that electrolyte-controlled electrowetting can recover the symmetric electrocapillary limit under appropriate conditions and establish a unified framework connecting double-layer structure, interfacial free energy, and voltage-dependent wetting.

title: A Microporous Zr-Tetraphosphonate MOF with Permanent Porosity, Robustness, and Thermochemical Heat Storage Capability
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Combining high-valent metal cations with phosphonate linkers represents a promising strategy to address the limited stability of MOFs, yet permanently porous phosphonate MOFs (P-MOFs) remain rare due to the strong coordination propensity of phosphonate groups. Herein, we report IEF-10, a new microporous zirconium tetraphosphonate framework constructed from ZrO5F octahedral secondary building units and a pyrene tetraphosphonate linker. The material combines three features that are seldom achieved simultaneously in P-MOFs: permanent accessible microporosity (equivalent BET surface area ∼430 m2·g–1), accessible phosphonic acid functionalities (-PO3H), and exceptional thermal (up to 450 °C), mechanical (>3 tons), and chemical stability (pH 1–12, organic solvents). The structure exhibits reversible water adsorption with moderate uptake and experimentally determined capacities of heat storage of ∼400–500 J·g–1, reflecting a favorable balance between host–guest interactions and regeneration requirements. As a proof of concept, IEF-10 was evaluated for thermochemical heat storage under dynamic moist-gas flow conditions. Calorimetric measurements revealed fast heat-release kinetics (3–4 h), and excellent cyclability in terms of heat release (at least 10 cycles, total test duration of 5 weeks). The hydrophobic surface character is an advantage for long-term storage uses as the adsorbent can remain in a dry state between the charging and discharging stages even at low relative humidity levels in the reactor. These results demonstrate how the combination of permanent porosity, accessible phosphonic acid groups, and exceptional framework robustness can enable functional adsorption-driven energy storage while providing new opportunities for the development of porous zirconium P-MOFs.

title: In situ formation of lithiophobic and tough grain boundary interphases for dendrite-resistant solid-state batteries
source: Joule

title: Singlet fission and triplet transfer to a metal halide perovskite absorber
source: Joule
abstract: Singlet fission in tetracene generates triplet excitons that are harvested by a metal halide perovskite through a ZnPc-mediated interface with energetics consistent with an interfacial hybrid charge-transfer (IHCT) pathway, enabling triplet sensitization and their contribution to photocurrent generation in perovskite photovoltaic devices.

title: Chloride-mediated SAM locking via ligand-exchange reaction enables 18.8% active-area efficiency and stable organic solar modules
source: Joule
abstract: The unstable ITO-SAM interface limits organic solar cell efficiency and stability. We introduce a molecular locking strategy using a vacuum-deposited InClx interlayer that triggers ligand exchange to form a robust multidentate In–O–P coordination network. This enhances SAM anchoring and coverage, delivering 20.4% efficiency in small-area cells and 18.8% active-area efficiency in modules, while enhancing device stability. This approach provides a generalizable interfacial platform that overcomes the efficiency-stability-scalability trilemma, paving a new pathway for advancing organic photovoltaics and beyond.

title: Monolayer photonic-crystal manganese halide gel scintillator for full-vision imaging
source: Matter
abstract: A monolayer photonic crystal integrated with a transparent manganese halide gel scintillator enhances the extraction of X-ray-excited light while preserving high spatial resolution. By combining X-ray computed tomography with structured-light scanning, the system enables a unified, spatially registered three-dimensional visualization of internal structures and external geometry.

title: Rational Ionomer Design Directs Hydrogenation Pathways and Reactant Accessibility in Electrochemical Nitrate Reduction
source: ACS Energy Letters: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Ionomer engineering offers a powerful yet underexplored strategy for electrochemical nitrate reduction (NO3RR), since the polymer tailors the microenvironment at the catalyst surface. Here, we rationally design high-performance ionomers by applying fixed-charge sign and hydration as design criteria. Synthetic anion-exchange ionomers (AEIs) enhance NO3– accessibility, and the highest AEI hydration is accompanied by a shift in the dominant hydrogenation pathway toward a favorable *H-mediated regime. Time-dependent attenuated total reflection surface-enhanced infrared absorption spectroscopy (ATR-SEIRAS) coupled with numerical simulation yields a 40.7-fold higher NO3– diffusion coefficient for the AEI than for Nafion. Potential-dependent in situ ATR-SEIRAS combined with kinetic isotope effect measurements and *H scavenging supports a pathway shift arising from a hydrated microenvironment enriched in free and weakly hydrogen-bonded water. The AEI-modified commercial Cu nanoparticle electrode reaches an NH3 yield rate of 13.8 mg h–1cm–2 and 98.0% Faradaic efficiency, positioning the fixed-charge sign and hydration as accessible design descriptors potentially transferable to other electrocatalytic reactions.

title: Cesium-Triiodide-Mediated Crystallization Regulation of Pure-Iodide Wide-Bandgap Perovskites Enables Perovskite-Silicon Tandem Solar Cells Exceeding 30% Efficiency
source: ACS Energy Letters: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Pure-iodide wide-bandgap (WBG) perovskites (∼1.68 eV) featuring eliminated photoinduced halide segregation are compelling top-cell absorbers for perovskite-silicon tandem solar cells. However, their complex crystallization readily induces heterogeneous composition and structural defects, hindering performance improvements in the resulting devices. Here, we develop a cesium triiodide (CsI3)-mediated strategy to regulate intermediate-phase evolution of pure-iodide WBG perovskites. The CsI3-derived precursor chemistry reconstructs Pb-I coordination networks, suppresses premature organic-dominated intermediate nucleation, and promotes homogeneous phase conversion. The modulated crystallization pathway yields highly crystalline films with improved iodine uniformity and reduced non-radiative recombination losses. Consequently, single-junction solar cells achieve a stabilized power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 22.40%, which retains 95% of its initial efficiency after 1500 h of maximum power point tracking. More importantly, the associated perovskite-silicon solar cells deliver a stabilized PCE of 30.74% along with improved thermal stability, highlighting the great potential of pure-iodide WBG perovskites for efficient and durable tandem photovoltaics.

title: Electrically Enabled Isothermal CeO2 Thermochemical Water Splitting below 900 °C
source: ACS Energy Letters: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Ceria-based thermochemical cycles offer a promising route to solar hydrogen, but require reduction above 1400 °C and large temperature swings. Here, building on electrically assisted CeO2 reduction, we demonstrate repeated isothermal CeO2-based water-splitting cycles at 700–900 °C and 0.5–2.0 V. Porous CeO2−YSZ bilayer pellets with different composition ratios undergo electrically assisted reduction and steam re-oxidation at the same temperature, producing O2 and H2 in separate steps without thermal cycling. The process reaches H2/O2 ratios up to 1.9, reproducible H2 productivity over 10 cycles, and H2 yields up to 49 ± 2 μmol gCeO2−1 cycle−1 after only 20 min of electrically assisted reduction. Extended-reduction experiments show that the best composition remains only ∼0.10 V below the applied bias on an equivalent thermodynamic-voltage basis. Reactor-scale projections based on gas utilization in an existing ceria reactor give a solar-to-H2 efficiency of 5.6% without assuming improvements to the CeO2−YSZ architecture.

title: Scalable Fluorinated Copper-Based Covalent Organic Frameworks for Coupled Ultratrace Perfluoroalkyl Substances Monitoring and Efficient Remediation
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are persistent water contaminants that require both effective removal and reliable monitoring. However, these functions are typically performed separately, preventing real-time evaluation of treatment performance. Here we establish a cooperative host–guest-coupling principle, in which a single host–guest binding event simultaneously drives contaminant capture and modulates the Cu-centered redox process, thereby generating concentration-dependent electrochemical signals within a porous framework. Guided by this principle, we reported a scalable fluorinated copper-based covalent organic framework (F–Cu–COF) synthesized through an open-air one-pot strategy that enables gram-scale production while retaining high crystallinity and chemical stability. Fluorinated pore domains and redox-active Cu centers create a cooperative host–guest environment that promotes PFAS binding and enrichment with electrochemical signal generation. Consequently, F–Cu–COF achieves a detection limit of 5.2 pg L–1, an uptake capacity of 3824 mg g–1, and efficient flow-through removal. This work establishes host–guest coupling as a common molecular basis for linking electrochemical signal generation with contaminant capture in scalable porous materials, providing a general design strategy for multifunctional water-treatment platforms capable of integrated treatment verification.

title: Support Protection Mechanism Enables Efficient and Stable Anion Exchange Membrane Water Electrolyzers
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Designing oxygen evolution reaction (OER) catalysts that simultaneously achieve high activity and long-term stability remains a critical challenge for the development of alkaline anion exchange membrane water electrolyzers (AEMWEs). Here, we uncover a unique support protection mechanism in which lattice-confined ruthenium (Ru) single atoms offer robust protection for the spinel Co3O4 support, realizing outstanding stability in AEMWEs. Theoretical calculations and structural characterizations reveal that lattice confinement promotes the formation of robust Ru–O–Co bridges by simultaneously shortening the Co–O and Ru–O bond lengths, thereby suppressing Co dissolution and optimizing the electronic structure for efficient catalysis. Furthermore, in situ electrochemical analysis demonstrates that the lattice confinement of Ru atoms accelerates OER kinetics through facilitated proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET) steps and partially activated lattice oxygen. As a result, the RuLCA-Co3O4 dominated by the adsorbate evolution mechanism (AEM) exhibits a lower overpotential of 260 mV at 10 mA cm–2, which is lower than that of RuSCA-Co3O4 dominated by the lattice oxygen mechanism (LOM) pathway. Meanwhile, the lattice-confined RuLCA-Co3O4 exhibits nearly 9-fold lower Co dissolution compared to surface-coordinated RuSCA-Co3O4 after an accelerated durability test (ADT). Moreover, RuLCA-Co3O4 maintains an outstanding stability for over 1000 h in an AEMWE system with a low degradation rate of 88.1 μV h–1, outperforming RuSCA-Co3O4. This work establishes lattice confinement as an effective strategy to decouple activity-stability trade-offs in alkaline OER and provides a viable design principle for durable AEMWE anodes.

title: G-Quadruplex-Interacting Photooxidative Platinum(IV) Prodrug for Inhibiting Oncogene Transcription and Amplifying Antitumor Immunity
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Conventional platinum (Pt)-based chemotherapeutics elicit cancer cell death primarily through DNA binding, but this approach is inherently limited by poor site specificity and a lack of spatiotemporal control, which compromises therapeutic precision and safety. To overcome these limitations, we report DNATplatin, an in situ activatable and photooxidative Pt(IV) prodrug designed to combine precise recognition of DNA secondary structures with targeted genetic intervention through DNA photooxidation. By incorporating a bis-N-methylpyridinium moiety to selectively recognize DNA, DNATplatin shows a 10-fold increase in the levels in genomic DNA relative to oxaliplatin and a 2.5-fold emission turn-on selectivity for G-quadruplexes (G4s) over typical duplex DNA. Following precise nuclear localization, photoactivated DNATplatin acts as a potent photooxidant that oxidizes G4, dismantles G4 scaffolds, and abrogates circular dichroism signatures. These orchestrated lesions generate localized oxidative stress and selectively silence major G4-driven oncogenes, thereby effectively circumventing traditional Pt resistance by bypassing canonical adduct-dependent pathways. In a murine triple-negative breast tumor model, DNATplatin produces profound tumor suppression and elicits a robust systemic immune response, characterized by CD4+/CD8+ T-cell activation and depletion of Foxp3+ regulatory T cells. Collectively, this work establishes a controllable “target-and-destroy” strategy and underscores the potential of Pt(IV) photooxidants for topology-selective genetic intervention.

title: Strain-Release Cycloadditions: Bicyclobutanes and Beyond
source: Chemical Reviews: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Strain-release cycloadditions have emerged as powerful reactions for converting distorted ring systems into complex and otherwise hardly attainable organic molecular architectures. This Review encompasses the fundamentals of strain, its role in governing cycloaddition pathways, and offers a systematic examination of strained carbocycles and heterocycles, from bicyclo[1.1.1]butanes and 1-azabicyclo[1.1.1]butanes, housanes and aza-housanes, 2H-azirines and aziridines, azetidines, cyclopropanes, cyclobutanes, oxiranes, oxetanes, and strained alkynes and alkenes. Across these motifs, the general principles that dictate reactivity, the breadth of known cycloadditions and activation strategies, from Brønsted and Lewis acid catalysis to transition-metal activation, photocatalysis, and double strain-release mechanisms, are highlighted. Key opportunities, current limitations, and future directions are outlined.

title: Decoupling Dissolution from Water Oxidation at Single-Faceted High-Entropy Perovskite Electrodes
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract High-entropy oxides (HEOs) are promising anode materials for the oxygen evolution reaction (OER) due to their wide compositional space and electronic flexibility. However, their electrochemical dissolution and OER remain concurrent, preventing decoupled analysis of dissolution kinetics and stability. Here, we present a combined atomic force microscopy (AFM) and scanning electrochemical cell microscopy (SECCM) strategy to decouple lattice dissolution from water oxidation under well-defined reaction conditions. Structurally analogous, atomically flat, single-faceted (001) ABO3 perovskite electrodes, La1–xSrx(Cr0.2Mn0.2Fe0.2Co0.2Ni0.2)O3 with x = 0 and 0.3, serve as model systems to probe dissolution and OER kinetics in acid. Pipet-probed localized cyclic voltammetry and chronoamperometry reveal that the measured current contains contributions from both OER and lattice dissolution, the latter producing nanoscale dissolution pits beneath the SECCM droplet. By correlating pit-growth kinetics with total OER charge as a function of pulse duration (τ), overpotential (η), and pH, we quantitatively separate dissolution from OER. The proportional scaling between dissolution charge and total charge indicates that OER and dissolution proceed within a common kinetic regime, sharing a common intermediate. A rate-law-based analysis yields the standard dissolution rate constant (kd0 cm/s), transfer coefficient (α), and proton reaction order (b) for the dissolution of the 001 facet of both HEO-P. Our results unravel how aliovalent A-site substitution (30% Sr2+) alters dissolution kinetics, charge partitioning between dissolution and OER, and thickness-dependent stability, thereby enabling quantitative disentangling of the intrinsic activity and stability of HEO electrodes.

title: Fluorine-Mediated Molten-Salt Crystallization Regulates Phase Evolution and Structural Stability in Sodium Layered Oxides
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Ni- and Co-free P2-type Fe–Mn layered oxides with high Na concentrations are promising cathodes for sodium-ion batteries, but their practical use is limited by phase instability during Na-excess synthesis and structural degradation during cycling and storage. Although large single-crystal-like architectures could improve stability, controlled phase-selective crystallization in these cathode systems remains challenging. Here, we show that fluorine-assisted molten-salt synthesis enables controlled formation of large-particle Fe–Mn–Ti P2 cathodes with enhanced phase selectivity and structural coherence. Compared with Na-excess processing alone, NaF-assisted flux growth expands the P2 phase stability window and promotes large particles with uniform morphologies while preserving local layered ordering. Multiscale characterization further reveals more-reversible structural evolution and more homogeneous Mn redox behavior in the NaF-assisted material, together with a gradient-like fluorine distribution involving surface-enriched NaF-like species and lower level interior fluorine environments. These coupled structural, morphological, and chemical features collectively mitigate crack formation and deliver good cycling stability. In summary, NaF-assisted molten-salt synthesis shows promise in addressing key limitations of Ni- and Co-free P2-type Fe–Mn layered cathodes.

title: Modifier-Driven Proton Conductivity in Hybrid Glasses above 200 °C
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Compositional tuning is a cornerstone of inorganic glass science, yet analogous strategies remain underdeveloped for emerging metal–organic hybrid glasses. We introduce phosphate modification of zinc imidazolate glass as a route to hybrid glasses with tunable network connectivity and proton-conductive functionality. Melt-quenching of ZIF-zni with benzimidazolium dihydrogen phosphate (BP) affords a series of cm-scale, transparent bulk glasses across a wide compositional range. Systematic characterization reveals that modification proceeds through ligand exchange at zinc centers, increasing the average coordination number from 4 to above 5 and progressively depolymerizing the imidazolate network. Despite macroscopic homogeneity, X-ray total scattering identifies a quasi-periodic ordering at ∼11 Å, and 1H NMR spin relaxation establishes nanoscale phase segregation between ZIF-derived and BP-rich domains of 2–70 nm. This heterogeneity underpins proton transport under anhydrous conditions; conductivities of 10–5–10–3 S cm–1 at 240 °C follow Vogel–Tammann–Fulcher dynamics, confirming that segmental motion couples to ion mobility. Infiltrating the glass into a porous PTFE scaffold yields a composite membrane that achieves 8.4 × 10–5 S cm–1 at 170 °C under humidification and sustains steam electrolysis with near-unity Faradaic efficiency. These results establish network-modified hybrid glasses as a scalable and designable platform for intermediate-temperature solid electrolytes.

title: Boosting Ionomer Oxygen Transport via Pore Confinement in Carbon Supports for Low-Pt Fuel Cells
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Low-Pt proton exchange membrane fuel cells (PEMFCs) are promising for hydrogen energy implementation, yet oxygen transport through ionomer-covered catalyst surfaces becomes increasingly limiting due to the resistance associated with dense ionomer films. Herein, we demonstrate a pore-confinement strategy to manipulate the spatial locality of Pt nanoparticles within porous carbon supports, enabling simultaneous regulation of ionomer distribution and molecular organization. Pt nanoparticles were selectively positioned on the external surfaces (Ptext/PC) or within the internal nanopores (Ptint/PC) of otherwise comparable supports, while maintaining similar Pt loading, particle size, and pore characteristics. Under H2-air condition, Ptint/PC delivered a peak power density ∼1.3 times higher than that of Ptext/PC, but a similar current density in the high-voltage region. Electrochemical analyses reveal that the performance enhancement originates from improved oxygen transport rather than catalytic activity. Wide-angle X-ray scattering and molecular dynamics simulations reveal that the Pt nanoparticles confined within mesopores disrupt the dense packing of ionomer backbones, thereby boosting oxygen permeability at the catalyst–ionomer interface. By establishing a direct relationship between Pt locality, ionomer distribution, backbone organization, and oxygen transport, this work identifies catalyst locality as an effective parameter for engineering interfacial mass transport and provides a new design principle for low-Pt PEMFCs.

title: Sky-Blue Thermally Activated Delayed Fluorescence from a Zirconium(IV) Complex
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Earth-abundant early transition-metal complexes with luminescent ligand-to-metal charge-transfer (LMCT) excited states remain an attractive yet underexplored alternative to widely used precious-metal emitters. A fundamental understanding of the molecular design principles governing the photophysical properties of LMCT emitters is critical to further developing cost-effective and sustainable photochemical applications using this compound class. Here, we report the synthesis of a novel bis(4,5-ditolylamido-9,9-dimethylxanthene)zirconium complex, Zr(TolXDA)2, that shows efficient photoluminescence due to thermally activated delayed fluorescence (TADF) at room temperature. Steady-state and time-resolved spectroscopic studies at room temperature reveal highly efficient and long-lived emission in the sky-blue and green wavelength range for solid samples (λPL = 480 nm, ΦPL = 0.60, τPL = 4–14 μs) and THF solutions (λPL = 548 nm, ΦPL = 0.30, τPL = 8 μs) of Zr(TolXDA)2, respectively. Despite the relatively large singlet–triplet energy gap (ΔEST ≥ 0.26 eV), TADF emission in Zr(TolXDA)2 is unambiguously confirmed by temperature-dependent emission studies. This is likely facilitated by the high LMCT character of the S1 and T1 states, a consequence of strategic ligand design, which allows for rapid forward and reverse intersystem crossing. This hypothesis is supported by femtosecond transient absorption spectroscopy, which confirms facile forward and reverse intersystem crossing in Zr(TolXDA)2 (τISC = 15 ± 5 ps, τrISC = 0.48 ± 0.39 μs), and TD-DFT calculations, which establish significant negative charge transfer to zirconium in the lowest energy excited states.

title: Enhancing Propanol Production from CO2 Reduction with a Terbium-Doped Copper Nitride Electrocatalyst
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Propanol is one of the most complex products obtained from CO2 electroreduction (CO2R). Being an interesting precursor for synthetic fuels and a feedstock for the chemical industry, its electrochemical production has recently raised increasing interest. However, low selectivity for propanol has been achieved so far. Here, via exploring a variety of original lanthanide-doped copper nitride materials, we identified and characterized terbium-doped copper nitride as the most selective catalyst for propanol formation. It allowed CO2R to yield propanol with a Faradaic efficiency of 27% at a high current density of 300 mA cm–2 within a neutral (KHCO3 electrolyte) flow cell, surpassing the performance of previous CO2R catalysts. The high density of undercoordinated nitride-derived Cu sites, combined with the increased oxophilicity of the surface, likely promoted the selectivity toward alcohols. Thorough DFT calculations showed that Tb doping increased the affinity for oxygenate-associated C2* intermediates and lowered the free-energy barrier for reactions coupling the latter with CO* toward propanol.

title: Kinetic Control of Polymorphism in Li10.5Si1.5P1.5S12–Based Solid Electrolytes
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Li10GeP2S12 (LGPS)-type solid electrolytes (SEs) are among the most promising materials for next-generation solid-state batteries (SSBs) due to their high lithium-ion conductivity. However, challenges related to phase stability and polymorphism, especially in Ge-free, Si-based systems, limit their practical implementation. Here, the crystallization and phase transition behavior of materials with a nominal composition of Li10.5–xSi1.5P1.5S12–xIx (x = 0, 0.2, 0.4) are systematically investigated. Operando high-temperature synchrotron X-ray diffraction, total scattering with pair distribution function analysis, and differential scanning calorimetry measurements reveal the formation of a metastable orthorhombic (o) phase, followed by transformation into the thermodynamically stable tetragonal (t) phase at elevated temperatures. Our findings indicate that lithium iodide (LiI) as an additive regulates the crystallization of the o-phase and thereby governs the transition kinetics. This enables the o-to-t phase transition to occur at much reduced temperatures and faster rates. Neutron powder diffraction further uncovers minor modifications to the Si/P ratio and lithium sublattice, as well as the fact that iodine is not incorporated into the t-phase; instead, a secondary Li4PS4I-type phase forms. Collectively, this work highlights the critical role of microstructural engineering on crystallization and polymorphism in LGPS-type SEs and also demonstrates the applicability of these dual-phase materials by enabling high-performance lithium–sulfur SSBs.

title: Core–Shell Structures Govern Through-Space Interactions in Triblock Copolymers toward Deep-Red Clusteroluminescence
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Green fluorescent protein (GFP) and its derivatives have transformed biological imaging, yet fluorophores that simultaneously combine biocompatibility, structural programmability, and intrinsic long-wavelength luminescence remain scarce. Here, we develop a controllable one-pot polymerization strategy to construct nonconjugated triblock copolymers that can self-assemble into core–shell clusters. By modulating the hydrophilic–hydrophobic balance of copolymer chains, the core-to-shell ratio, chain packing, and electronic through-space interactions within the clusters can be precisely regulated, enabling tunable clusteroluminescence (CL) that extends to the deep-red and near-infrared emission region. Ultrafast spectroscopy further uncovers the excited-state dynamics of these core–shell clusters and reveals how the coupled evolution of electronic states and structures governs CL generation. Moreover, the core–shell clusters enable in vivo angiography under two-photon excitation, highlighting their potential as biocompatible nanofluorophores. These findings establish core–shell engineering as a general design principle for efficient clusteroluminogens, deepen the mechanistic understanding of CL, and pave the way for next-generation nanofluorescence technologies.

title: Intricate Proteoform Heterogeneity in the Tailpiece of IgA within and across Its Circulatory and Secretory Configurations
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Human immunoglobulin A (IgA) naturally occurs in multiple molecular forms─monomers, dimers, and even higher-order polymers─that are differentially distributed across serum, breast milk, and mucosal surfaces. The C-terminal tailpiece of IgA is essential to its polymerization mediated by the joining chain (J-chain) and thus also an important determinant of its extensive structural heterogeneity, yet its features remain somewhat poorly defined. Here, we used HILIC-LC-MS/MS-based glycopeptide analysis to characterize the N-glycan structures, disulfide linkages, and C-terminal amino acid sequence variants within the IgA tailpiece across the different molecular configurations of endogenous IgA. We find extensive correlation between these post-translational modifications; i.e., variations in tailpiece Asn459 N-glycosylation, redox status and disulfide connectivity of Cys471, and the presence or absence of C-terminal Tyr472 are intrinsically interconnected. When Cys471 was disulfide-bound to the J-chain, Asn459 glycans showed broader structural heterogeneity and retained more high-mannose structures, whereas free Cys471 tailpieces mainly carried mature, sialylated complex-type glycans. Serum IgA and milk SIgA displayed distinct tailpiece signatures, including differences in N-glycan maturation and processing of the ultimate C-terminal Tyr472 residue. Together, these findings define biofluid-specific molecular forms of IgA and highlight the remarkable structural diversity of the human IgA tailpiece. Overall, our results advance the understanding of the IgA structure and could offer a much-needed molecular basis to assist future bioengineering of IgA-based therapeutics.

title: Synthetic W/Cu Mimics of the Mo/Cu Active Site in Aerobic CODH: Nonclassical Isocyanide Coordination and the Role of the Bridging Sulfide
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Aerobic carbon monoxide dehydrogenase (CODH) uses an unsupported Mo–S–Cu heterobimetallic active site to catalyze CO oxidation, but the mechanistic role of the bridging sulfide remains to be fully resolved. We report a series of W/Cu complexes designed to test whether steric shielding from a bidentate tBuxantphos ligand can suppress unwanted Cu···Sdithiolate and Cu···O═M interactions that plagued the reactivity of a previously reported NHC-ligated model system. Addition of [Cu(tBuxantphos)]+ to [(bdt)WVI(O)(OSiiPr3)(X)]− (bdt = 1,2-benzenedithiolate; X = O, S, Se) unexpectedly favors Cu coordination at the W═O rather than the W═X unit, giving X═W–O–Cu cores as the thermodynamically preferred isomers, opposite to the connectivity predicted by hard–soft acid–base theory and found in CODH itself. The resulting complexes bind isocyanides at CuI with nonclassical (blue-shifted) C≡N stretching frequencies. In contrast, no reactivity is observed toward CO gas, consistent with DFT predictions that CO coordination is endergonic. However, the calculations reveal that the CO adduct of the hypothetical O═W–S–Cu–CO isomer is more stabilized than its S═W–O–Cu–CO counterpart, an effect traced by molecular orbital analysis to delocalization of electron density from the redox-active dithiolate through the bridging sulfide into the Cu–CO π-backbonding manifold. These results provide an electronic rather than purely structural rationale for why the CODH active site retains a bridging sulfide despite an apparent thermodynamic preference for a bridging oxo in the synthetic analogues investigated here.

title: Interhalogen of Iodine Chloride Accelerates Charge Transfer for Efficient Li2O2 Oxidation in Lithium–Oxygen Batteries
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Li–O2 batteries suffer from sluggish Li2O2 oxidation kinetics at electrode/electrolyte interfaces, leading to large charge polarization and low energy efficiency. Soluble redox mediators (RMs) provide a solution-mediated pathway for Li2O2 decomposition and reduce the charge overpotential. However, the chemical oxidation of Li2O2 by oxidized RMs remains kinetically sluggish, resulting in persistent charge polarization. Herein, iodine monochloride (ICl), an interhalogen compound, is electrochemically generated in situ during the charge process to promote the oxidation of Li2O2.
